description: In the Mainstream Voucher program, the PHA has traditionally been required to  demonstrate in its application a need for these vouchers by providing information documenting that the demand for housing for non-elderly persons with disabilities would equal or exceed the requested number of vouchers. Currently, most Mainstream Voucher programs are relatively small and do not support a separate division by itself in a PHA’s organizational record. Typically, staff that work on the HCV program (i.e., waitlist, recertification, inspection functions) perform the same required functions for the Mainstream Voucher Program. If the PHA does not have a separate accounting for Accounting Brief #25: FDS Reporting Guidance for the Mainstream Voucher Program, then the PHA will need to account for the Mainstream Voucher Program costs using a reasonable cost allocation method as required under 2 CFR 200. PHAs should not use a fee concept in determining the administrative costs of the Mainstream Voucher Program where the PHA’s HCV Program would charge a set fee to the Mainstream Voucher Program regardless of the actual costs incurred by the Mainstream Voucher Program. The use of the fee concept incorrectly assumes that all administrative fees earned by the Mainstream Voucher Program is the actual cost of the program. As such, a fee methodology could result in an overstatement of the HCV program administrative expenses, and the actual costs of the HCV and Mainstream Voucher Program would be co-mingled in the HCV Program.

overview.objective:
This listing is comprised of two components: (1) the Lead-Based Paint Capital Fund program (LBP) and Housing-Related Hazards (HRH) Capital Fund program, referred to jointly as the LBP and HRH Capital Fund program; and (2) the Capital Improvements for At-Risk/ Receivership/ Substandard/ Troubled program (At-Risk program).
Competitive grants are provided for Public Housing Authorities (PHAs) for the modernization of public housing developments, with a focus on housing-related health and safety hazards that may contribute to illness, injury or other adverse health outcomes for public housing residents.
1.	LBP and HRH program funds can be used in one or both of the following focus areas: 
a.	Lead-Based Paint Focus: evaluate and reduce lead-based paint hazards in public housing specifically by carrying out the activities of lead-based risk assessments, inspections, abatement, interim controls, clearance examinations, and relocation. 
b.	General Housing-Related Hazards Focus: evaluate and reduce housing-related hazards including mold, radon, carbon monoxide, and fire safety hazards in public housing.
2.	Capital Fund At-Risk program funds are for PHAs in receivership, designated troubled or substandard, or otherwise at risk, to support the costs associated with public housing asset improvement.

overview.objective:
The Choice Neighborhoods program transforms severely distressed public housing and the surrounding area. Choice Neighborhoods Implementation Grants provide funding to carry out locally driven “Transformation Plans.” The Transformation Plan is a comprehensive revitalization strategy for an identified “target housing” project(s) and “target neighborhood.” Implementation Grantees use the grant funds, plus other public and private money, to redevelop the target public housing project(s), help residents become self-sufficient, and revitalize neighborhoods. The program has three main goals:  

Housing: Redevelop severely distressed public housing into good quality, mixed-income housing that meets residents’ needs and helps revitalize the community 

People: Help residents in the public housing improve their lives through upward mobility, employment, and self-sufficiency 

Neighborhood: Revitalize distressed neighborhoods by attracting long-term reinvestment from private and other public sources, leading to economic development better amenities, services, and job opportunities for residents

overview.objective:
This funding opportunity supports the establishment of a National Fund Manager (NFM) to design and administer a Lead-Safe and Healthy Homes Fund Demonstration. The purpose of this initiative is to create the first national financing facility that aggregates public and private capital to accelerate the reduction of residential lead hazards and advance the eradication of childhood lead poisoning. Authorized under Sections 501 and 502 of the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1970 and funded through the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, the program seeks to leverage federal resources at a minimum 4-to-1 ratio to expand investment in lead hazard control and healthy housing interventions.

The National Fund Manager will raise and assemble capital, develop financial products such as credit enhancements and loan guarantees, and partner with community development organizations to expand access to grants and loans for low- and moderate-income households. By mobilizing private sector investment alongside public funding, the program aims to accelerate lead hazard remediation, complement existing HUD and EPA programs, and strengthen national capacity to address housing-related health and safety hazards.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
This program supports the creation of a National Lead-Safe and Healthy Homes Financing Fund to help communities reduce residential lead hazards and prevent childhood lead poisoning. Through this initiative, HUD will select a National Fund Manager to raise and combine public and private funding and make those resources available to local organizations working to make homes safer and healthier, particularly for low- and moderate-income families.

The program serves community development organizations, local governments, housing providers, and other partners that assist homeowners and landlords in addressing lead-based paint and related housing health hazards. By leveraging private sector investment alongside federal funds, this initiative expands the resources available for lead hazard control beyond traditional grant programs.

financialInformation.additionalInformation:
This program is actively funded in the current fiscal year through an appropriation specifically provided by the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 (Public Law 118-42), which includes approximately $8 million allocated to establish and operationalize a Lead-Safe and Healthy Homes Fund Demonstration by selecting a National Fund Manager. The program remains in active status because Congress has appropriated dedicated funds for this purpose, and HUD’s Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes (OLHCHH) continues to issue competitive notices of funding opportunities to carry out the goals of mitigating residential lead hazards and leveraging public and private capital to accelerate lead hazard control nationwide.

Even though this is a new initiative, the program builds on HUD’s ongoing investments in lead hazard reduction and healthy homes activities, which have historically received significant appropriations and continue to be part of HUD’s strategic funding portfolio. Discrepancies between historical obligations and obligations reported on USAspending.gov may occur because past funds obligated under related lead and healthy homes grant programs (such as traditional Lead Hazard Control and Lead Hazard Reduction Demonstration grants) were awarded under earlier Assistance Listings or CFDA numbers, whereas this specific Fund demonstration represents a new financing mechanism with distinct appropriation and reporting cycles. Because those prior obligations were captured under different listings and fiscal years, they may not directly align with the current listing’s obligation data on USAspending.gov.

overview.objective:
The Experienced Services Program (ESP) provides support to the National Park Service (NPS) on natural and cultural resource conservation projects that enable the agency to carry out its mission. Special emphasis will be placed on projects that improve the maintenance of national park resources and enhance the visitor experience.

ESP participants will provide technical assistance and support to the NPS in the development and execution of projects that benefit the general public and provide support to NPS employees. This program will provide opportunities to qualified individuals 55 years of age and older, who have specific technical skills and abilities not available or underrepresented at current NPS staffing levels. The ESP participants will not replace or displace current NPS employees.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Experienced Services Program (ESP) brings in highly experienced individuals—age 55 or older—to help the National Park Service carry out important work that benefits parks, public lands, and the public. Through time‑limited, project‑based assignments, participants provide specialized skills that support natural and cultural resource protection, facility maintenance, visitor services, planning, emergency preparedness, and other critical functions. Their expertise strengthens the agency’s ability to maintain safe, well‑cared‑for parks while expanding capacity where staffing or technical skill gaps exist.

list.description:
Projects provide opportunities for experienced individuals to contribute their skills and knowledge, including mentoring staff, providing technical expertise, and supporting various projects across different departments --

1) Engineering Projects: Funding supports electrical, geotechnical, and civil engineering tasks, including infrastructure improvements, safety enhancements, and regulatory compliance.

2) Historical Architecture: Funds aid in preserving and restoring historical buildings, mentoring new architects, and ensuring historical accuracy.

3) Environmental Compliance: Funding is used for environmental impact assessments, regulatory compliance, and mitigation measures.

4) Fire Protection: Funds support fire safety system design, risk assessments, and compliance with fire safety standards.

5) Project Management: Funding assists in developing project plans, stakeholder coordination, and ensuring timely and budget-compliant project completion.

Projects provide opportunities for experienced individuals to contribute their skills and knowledge, including mentoring staff, providing technical expertise, and supporting various projects across different departments --

1. Preserving Historic Buildings and Sites -- Funding is used to hire skilled workers who inspect old buildings, figure out what repairs are needed, and make sure the repairs follow rules for preserving history.

2. Protecting Natural and Cultural Resources -- Funding is used to hire experts who help protect wildlife, manage fire safety, and preserve cultural sites. These specialists make sure parks follow safety codes, protect visitors and staff, and maintain important resources like archives and collections.

3. Improving Visitor Experience -- Funding supports projects that make parks more accessible and enjoyable. This includes maintaining trails, improving facilities, and providing educational programs. Workers help ensure parks are welcoming, safe, and informative for everyone.

4. Providing Training and Technical Support -- Funding is used to bring in trainers and technical experts who teach staff and volunteers important skills, such as CPR, first aid, and proper maintenance techniques. This helps parks operate efficiently and safely.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: Accomplishments include utilizing Experienced Services Program (ESP) enrollee engineers to provided critical expertise in maintaining and improving park infrastructure, ensuring safety and sustainability; historical architecture support to help maintain the integrity of historical structures and pass on valuable skills to the next generation of architects; historic sites preservation and compliance with preservation standards, benefiting communities and preserving history; and fire protection engineers to design and implement fire safety systems, conduct fire risk assessments, and ensure that buildings and facilities meet fire safety standards.

ESP participants contributed to dozens of projects across national parks, monuments, and regional offices. Collectively, these projects helped parks operate safely, protect cultural and natural resources, improve visitor experiences, and complete specialized work that requires seasoned professionals.

1. Protecting Natural and Cultural Resources -- ESP participants played a key role in preserving historic places, caring for museum archives, improving documentation of archeological sites, and supporting environmental restoration. Their work included assessing damage from environmental incidents, preparing historic structures for preservation projects, and improving the treatment and long-term care of collections.

2. Strengthening Park Operations and Safety -- Many parks used ESP participants to support daily operations that keep parks open and safe. They performed road maintenance and snow removal, supported fire prevention and structural fire compliance, maintained remote weather stations, and provided heavy equipment expertise for erosion control and trail access improvements. These efforts increased safety for visitors, employees, and emergency responders.

3. Supporting Major National Initiatives -- ESP participants contributed to high‑visibility national projects, including efforts associated with America’s 250th anniversary. They provided project management, archival support, and coordination for events, ensuring that parks are prepared to engage the public in meaningful national commemorations.

4. Enhancing Administrative and Technical Capacity -- Parks also relied on ESP participants to strengthen internal functions such as Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) processing, travel and charge card compliance, GIS support, data tracking, and program analysis. These contributions helped parks meet federal requirements, reduce backlogs, and operate more efficiently.

overview.objective: This program will give Alaska Native students the opportunity to learn about the importance of BOEM's mission to manage the development of US Outer Continental Shelf energy and mineral resources while exploring future career options with BOEM. Assignments will be designed to provide orientation and experience in the practical application of the theories, concepts and principles of petroleum engineering, geology, geophysics, and/or environmental science. The Alaska Native Science and Engineering Program (ANSEP) is designated as tax exempt under the IRS for Institutions of Higher Education. Established in 1995, ANSEP has evolved into a longitudinal education model that provides a continuous string of components beginning with students in sixth grade and continuing through high school, into science and engineering undergraduate and graduate degree programs through PhD.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Recipient of the assistance is the Alaska Native Science and Engineering Program (ANSEP), and the assistance must be used to provide work and training opportunities to young people between the ages of 16 and 25, working on appropriate conservation projects associated with oil and gas and marine mineral development on the outer continental shelf (OCS) within the BOEM area of responsibility. The majority of funds will be used to support projects that will enhance understanding of energy exploration and production techniques and related impacts to support development of U.S. OCS energy and mineral resources in an environmentally and economically responsible way. Classroom and on-the- job training in stewardship of U.S. OCS energy and mineral resources. Training provides experience in the practical application of basic principles techniques, and concepts of petroleum engineering, geology, geophysics, and environmental science. Funds not used for capitalization.

overview.objective: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement and plan forest, rangeland, and watershed restoration projects by facilitating partnerships with authorized states, counties, and federally recognized Indian tribes. The GNA authority specifically allows BLM to enhance state-federal relationships and addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include treating insect-and disease-infested trees; reducing hazardous fuels; any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat.  This type of work has reduced wildfire risk to habitat, communities, and state trust lands; creates greater forest and watershed resilience against drought, insects, disease, and wildfire and expands much-needed work across state and federal lands.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA)-Restoration is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement and plan forest, rangeland, and watershed restoration projects by facilitating partnerships with authorized states, counties, and federally recognized Indian tribes.  The GNA specifically allows BLM to enhance government to government relationships and addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include treating insect-and disease-infested trees; reducing hazardous fuels; any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat.  This type of work has reduced wildfire risk to habitat and communities; creates greater forest and watershed resilience against drought, insects, disease, and wildfire and expands much-needed work across state and federal lands.  Authorized Restoration Services encompasses a broad set of restoration actions that work apply to work conducted by many BLM programs.  Examples of work that could be accomplished through the GNA-Restoration include but are not limited to: fuel breaks, herbicide application, seed and seedling planting, post-fire burned area rehabilitation, salvage/sanitation timber sales, pre-commercial/commercial thinning, prescribed fire, targeted grazing to meet rangeland health objectives, proactive forest or range restoration to provide wildlife habitat and improve livestock forage, noxious weed and invasive species treatments, wildland-urban interface fuels reduction, and community assistance to reduce the impacts of wildfire on the landscape, riparian or upland restoration as well as NEPA analysis and document preparation, endangered species act or cultural clearances, and data collection when conducted in conjunction with an authorized restoration service.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Experienced Service Program (ESP) is a federal initiative designed to bring the valuable knowledge, skills, and experience of older Americans into the work of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). As the BLM oversees millions of acres of public lands across the United States, it relies on a workforce with deep understanding of natural resources, cultural heritage, recreation management, environmental protection, and more. Over time, many of the people who have shaped this work retire, and with them goes critical institutional knowledge. ESP helps bridge that gap. ESP serves two main groups: 1. Older Americans looking to continue contributing their skills. Under the authority provided to the Department of the Interior, the BLM partners with nonprofit organizations designated by the Secretary of Labor under Title V of the Older Americans Act. These organizations specialize in creating pathways for older adults to remain active in the workforce, share their expertise, and take part in meaningful work that benefits their communities and the nation. 2. BLM programs and offices that need experienced talent. Many BLM programs—such as energy development, cultural and natural resources, recreation, grazing, forestry, and environmental compliance—can benefit from specialized experience. ESP placements help bolster capacity in these offices, especially in areas where retirements have created significant losses in institutional knowledge. Several features set ESP apart from other federal service or workforce programs: 1. A focus on older, highly experienced professionals Unlike many workforce or volunteer programs that target students or early-career individuals, ESP is specifically intended to leverage the talents of older Americans. These participants bring decades of practical knowledge and professional expertise that can be otherwise difficult to replace. 2. Flexible project-based support Assignments through ESP are tailored to match both BLM needs and participant strengths. This flexibility makes ESP highly responsive—projects can receive precisely the level and type of expertise needed without lengthy hiring processes or permanent staffing changes. 3. Partnership-driven model ESP uses a cooperative agreement structure, working through nonprofit organizations that specialize in serving and placing older adults. This model supports efficient recruitment, onboarding, and participant support.  4. Benefits to local communities Many ESP participants live in or near the communities where they serve. Their work supports local economies, strengthens public-land partnerships, and provides opportunities for older adults to remain active and engaged.

list.description:
Civil Engineering Technical Support- The purpose of the award is to support the engineering work needed to meet national timber program goals and maintain healthy forests.  This position contributes directly to preparing timber sales, including green timber, burned timber, and stands affected by forest pathogens.  This work strengthens the district's ability to meet annual timber targets, advance stewardship projects, and reduce hazardous fuels.  It also supports the sustained yield management direction for Oregon and California lands and helps implement recent directives that expand timber production across public lands.

Forestry Technician - The award supports caring for forests on public lands in Idaho. The project’s purpose is to gather reliable field information, lay out timber sales in a safe and efficient way, and prepare sites for harvest treatments so land stewards can make sound decisions. The goals are straightforward: measure trees and forest conditions, set clear boundaries and access routes for harvest areas, monitor sale activities, and keep simple, accurate records. The work strengthens forest health, improves planning, and ensures tasks are finished by the dates set by managers. The project enrollee completes hands-on field work across the Boise district and the Shoshone field office. Core actions include counting and measuring trees, recording conditions, and marking treatment areas. The enrollee helps design sale layouts, supports sale monitoring, and prepares sites by flagging plots and organizing tools and materials. The enrollee keeps a shared spreadsheet of hours and accomplishments and meets with the technical advisor and forester every two weeks to review progress. The work involves routine driving to field sites, occasional overnight camping during longer assignments, and the safe use of provided equipment and protective gear.

Oil and Gas Leasing Coordinator - The award supports the administration of Federal oil and gas leases under Title 43, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 3100 to strengthen domestic energy production and the collection of royalties for the United States. It advances national security, energy independence, and efficient governance by improving how lease cases are processed, reducing delays and errors, and ensuring that oil and gas resources on public lands are managed responsibly. The project supports and directly facilitates implementation of Executive Order 14154 and Secretarial Order 3418, “Unleashing American Energy.” Awarded under the Experienced Services Program, it engages an experienced enrollee to guide and train staff so the team completes cases accurately, applies consistent standards, and resolves complex issues with confidence.

Petroleum Engineer - The purpose of this award is to review and process oil and gas project requests. This support will keep important energy work moving forward and prevent delays. It will also help BLM follow national orders to support safe and responsible energy development. Activities to be performed: review applications from oil and gas companies, including unit requests, communitization agreements, participating areas, and drilling permits. Check reports and maps to make sure information is correct and complete. Talk with companies when information is missing or when plans need changes. Help solve technical problems and suggest better ways to complete projects. Recommend whether applications should be approved or denied. Review engineering documents and enter needed updates into agency systems.  Help identify possible issues using basic engineering and economic ideas.  Assist with bond reviews and other lease requirements.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), Public Law 93-638, encourages Indian self-determination and tribal control over services. Through the Consolidated Tribal Government program, tribes can merge similar services for greater flexibility in planning and meeting community needs. This approach combines multiple programs or grants into a single agreement, streamlining contracting and reducing paperwork and administrative costs. As a result, tribes can provide more impactful services with Bureau funds, such as, Scholarships, Johnson O'Malley, Adult Education, and Job Placement and Training.

overview.objective: To further the goals of Tribal Self-Governance compacting for Tribes to administer a wide rage of programs with broad administrative and programmatic flexibility.   The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA) authorizes Tribes and Tribal organizations to be funded by the Federal government to provide services that the Federal government would otherwise be obligated to provide due to the trust responsibilities and treaty obligations of the United States. ISDEAA establishes Self-Determination contracting (Title 1) and Self-Governance compacting (Title IV) as two unique options that Tribal governments can elect to use to assume control and decision-making authority over select federal programs and resources benefiting their citizens and communities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Tribal Self-Governance Program authorizes participating tribes to enter into self-governance compacts and funding agreements through which they may provide programs, services, functions, and activities the federal government would otherwise provide.  Through self-governance agreements, Federal law authorizes greater flexibility for participating tribes to shape programs to meet the unique social, economic, and cultural needs of their respective citizens.

list.description: Funds may be used by the Tribe/Consortium to provide a wide range of programs, services and activities such as social services, law enforcement, tribal courts, scholarships, social services, road maintenance and construction, forestry, agriculture, real estate services, wildlife and parks, employment and training. Except where a statute contains specific limitation on the use of funds, a Tribe/Consortium may redesign or consolidate programs included in a compact funding agreement and reallocate funds for such programs in any manner which it deems to be in the best interest of the Indian community being served.

overview.objective: To provide funds to Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and to tribal organizations to fund some or all of the indirect costs incurred in administering Federal programs for which direct appropriations are made to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), Public Law 93-638, provides that a Tribe is entitled to receive contract support costs as provided by law pursuant to 25 U.S.C. Section 5325. This applies to Indian Affairs contracts and agreements under made under Title I and Title IV of the ISDEAA. All costs associated with a program, including CSC, must be reviewed for reasonableness, allowability, and allocability based on the terms of the agreement and applicable cost principals. Further, all costs associated with a program, including CSC must be reviewed for duplication of funding for cost among cost categories, the Section 106(a)(1) amount (Secretarial Amount), Direct CSC, Indirect CSC, Pre-award CSC, and Start-up CSC.

list.description: Funds are for direct, indirect, pre-award, and start up eligible contract support costs

The ISDEAA authorizes funding for four types of Contract Support Cost: Pre-award, Start-up, direct, and indirect. Pre-award CSC are costs incurred before the start of an agreement. Start-up CSC are costs incurred on a one-time basis during the initial year that an agreement is in effect. Direct CSC are costs incurred in connection with direct administration of the program. Indirect CSC are additional administrative or other expenses related to the overhead incurred by the Tribal contractor in connection with the operation of the contracted program, within the Tribal contractor’s negotiated indirect cost pool.

overview.objective: These programs assist Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments by providing the resources necessary to develop a self-sustaining economic base. The program provides opportunities for business development, the coordination and integration of programs throughout the Federal government, and the partnering of Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments with local government and the public and private business sector.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
Assistance Listing Number (ALN) 15.032, titled Indian Economic Development, is a program run by the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Office of Indian Economic Development (OIED). Its purpose is to help Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments build strong, self-sustaining economies. It achieves this by supporting a broad range of economic initiatives from business startups and language support systems to strategic planning and tourism. This program focuses on tribal-led economic solutions and fostering collaborative partnerships with federal, state, local, and private-sector entities.

The Indian Business Incubators Program (IBIP) provides funding to established Business Incubators to serve Native entrepreneurs with start-up, early-stage, and established businesses who will provide products or services to Tribal reservation communities. These incubators offer mentorship, technical assistance, networking, and facilitate access to capital. IBIP grants support up to three years of incubation services, with possible extensions contingent upon continued appropriations and other factors.

The Living Languages Grant Program (LLGP) supports efforts to revitalize Native languages by funding immersion, education, and curriculum development initiatives, especially for tribal communities whose students are not served by Bureau of Indian Education (BIE) schools. The LLGP Native language immersion programming supports language revitalization efforts based on the unique needs of the awardee, aiming to enhance economic and community resilience through language revitalization efforts. 

Several specialized grant programs are currently authorized to meet targeted economic development in tourism. The Tribal Tourism Grant Program (TTGP) strives to provide substantial community benefits by facilitating and strengthening Tribal tourism activities, enhancing visitor experiences, and increasing visibility and access to Tribal destinations. These projects are supported through the NATIVE Act Cooperative Agreement, which facilitates federal technical assistance and regional coordination to promote sustainable Tribal tourism. The TTGP is distinct in that it does not fund the creation of entirely new tourism ventures, instead, it improves and grows what is already in place, ensuring projects align with tribal economic priorities.

Together, these programs under ALN 15.032 offer a coordinated toolkit for tribal nations to lead economic and cultural revitalization in ways tailored to their unique goals. By combining tourism growth (via TTGP and the NATIVE Act), entrepreneurial support (via IBIP), and cultural empowerment (via LLGP), the Assistance Listing enables tribes to steer their own economic development with culturally aligned, professionally supported grant programs.

list.description: The Indian Business Incubators Grant Program (IBIP) funded Business Incubators located on or near Tribal communities which provided business and entrepreneurs individually tailored training, networking and access to capital. The Living Languages Grant Program (LLGP) funded Native language immersion programming to support language revitalization efforts based on the unique needs of the awardee.

The IBIP, Tribal Tourism Grant Program (TTGP) and the NATIVE Act Cooperative Agreement programs have not yet selected projects for funding. The IBIP program anticipates funding projects that fund established Business Incubators to serve Native entrepreneurs with start-up, early-stage, and established businesses who will provide products or services to Tribal reservation communities. The TTGP program anticipates funding projects to achieve substantial community benefits by facilitating and strengthening Tribal tourism activities, enhancing visitor experiences, and increasing visibility and access to Tribal destinations. The NATIVE Act Cooperative Agreement program anticipates funding an entity to support TTGP and Office of Native Hawaiian Relations (ONHR) applicants, which is comprised of Tribes, Tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian organizations, by identifying technical assistance needs and delivering targeted capacity-building support to expand cultural heritage tourism and increase visitation.

title: Minerals and Mining on Indian Lands

overview.objective: The objectives of the Energy and Mineral Development Program are to: (1) provide funds to Tribes to perform technical evaluations of the energy (both renewable and conventional) and mineral resource potential of Indian reservations; (2) provide Tribes with geological, geophysical and engineering reports, maps, and other data concerning their energy and mineral resources; (3) provide Tribes technical assistance on using and interpreting assessment information so that Tribes can understand and plan for the potential development of these resources; and (4) provide Tribes with an outreach vehicle to promote their lands and resources to potential partners if they so desire.  Those projects that fell into economic development categories will be considered for funding through the Office of Indian Energy and Economic Development.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Energy and Mineral Development Program (EMDP) grant provides Federally recognized Tribal entities and Tribal Energy Development Organizations with financial assistance to identify, evaluate, and assess energy and mineral resources on Indian land. The program supports projects that conduct resource inventories, assessments, feasibility studies, and other pre development analyses necessary to plan for the processing, use, and development of Tribal energy and mineral resources.

Eligible resources and potential uses include, but are not limited to: biomass (woody and waste) for heat or electricity; transportation fuels; hydroelectric power; geothermal heating or electricity generation; district heating; distributed energy systems; oil, natural gas, and helium; sand and gravel; coal; precious minerals; and base minerals such as lead, copper, and zinc.

Pre development studies funded through EMDP are essential for Tribal leaders to make informed decisions about resource development and to advance projects to a stage where they can pursue financing. This no cost match program reduces project risk and supports early stage project development, helping build long term economic growth in Tribal communities. Energy and mineral resources remain among the most significant sources of economic opportunity on Tribal lands.

selectionCriteria.description:
Energy and Mineral Assessments: Proposals are evaluated according to technical merits of the mandatory elements of the proposal.  Additionally, selection criteria for ranking contain six criteria: (1) Resource Potential; (2) Commodity Marketability; (3) Economic Benefit, (4) Willingness to Develop and Commitment to the Project; (5) Budget Completeness, Cost Reasonableness, Cost Realism, and Detail, and (6) Adequacy of the Technical Proposal and Statement of Work.

Applications are scored on the clarity of its executive summary, the status and commitment behind the overarching project, the viability of its economic or financial impacts, the alignment and quality of its scope of work and deliverables, and the clarity and justification of its budget.

selectionCriteria.description: Funding levels for Real Estate Services and Real Estate Appraisals are determined by the individual Tribe through participation in the BIA's budget formulation process. All applicants meeting the criteria in 25 CFR Part 900 will be funded. Appraisals are conducted for all transactions involving trust property. The time required to complete an appraisal depends on the number of requests being processed by a specific office and the resources available to meet the requests. Lease Compliance funds are distributed to the Regional offices based on three factors: (1) total number of leases, (2) total number of acres, and (3) total amount of income derived from leases. Awards for lease compliance are determined by the number of qualifying leases reported to the Agency and Regional Offices. Minimum funding of $50,000 is allocated to each Regional office. In allocating program resources, priority is given to activities involving agriculture, oil and gas, mining, industrial, business, recreational, and other income-producing leases.

awardProcedure.description: For Real Estate Services and Real Estate Appraisals, the dollar value of the awards depends upon the amount that has been prioritized by the individual Tribe through tribal participation in the BIA's budget formulation process.  For Lease Compliance, funding is distributed to the Regional offices on the basis of number of existing leases and the number of inspections planned for the year.  For Lease Compliance awards, in some cases, the award can be approved at the agency level.  In most instances, the application will be forwarded to the Regional Director for approval.

overview.objective: The Family And Child Education (FACE) program is designed to serve families with children from prenatal to age 5 in home and center-based settings.  Families may receive services in one or both settings.  FACE provides early childhood for all children from birth - to age five and adult education for their parents through family literacy, parental involvement, increasing school readiness, high school graduation rates among Indian parents, and encouraging life-long learning.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Family and Child Education (FACE) program is a comprehensive family literacy program that serves eligible American Indian families with children from the prenatal stage through age five. The program strengthens families by providing integrated services through Family Enrichment (home-based), Prekindergarten, and Adult Education, recognizing parents and caregivers as a child's first and most important teachers. Families may participate in one or more program components based on their needs.
FACE is designed to improve school readiness, strengthen parent and family engagement in education, support healthy child development, and increase educational opportunities for both children and adults. Through culturally responsive instruction and family-centered services, the program promotes early language and literacy development, parenting education, adult education, and positive parent-child interactions that support lifelong learning.
What makes FACE unique is its multigenerational approach to education. Rather than focusing solely on the child, the program supports the entire family by combining high-quality early childhood education with adult learning opportunities and parent education. This coordinated approach helps families build the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed to support their children's success in school while advancing their own educational and personal goals. By strengthening the home learning environment and fostering meaningful partnerships between families, schools, and communities, FACE helps create a strong foundation for lifelong academic achievement and family well-being.

SAM.gov just limitted to 2000 character the following is what was posted in SAM.gov
Attorney Fee funds may be used only for legal fees (not expenses) of private legal counsel retained by tribes to represent them in litigation, negotiations, or administrative proceedings involving the protection of tribal trust resources or tribal rights. Although the Department of the Interior generally does not use federally appropriated funds to pay for private counsel representing Indian tribes, 25 CFR 89.40 provides limited exceptions. To qualify, a request must fully satisfy at least one exception listed in 25 CFR 89.41, identify the applicable exception(s), and explain how each is met. Approved funding is limited to a maximum rate of $200 per hour.
Each request must include:
1.	Historical background and other relevant information leading to the current matter.
2.	A concise description of the issue and scope of work for which attorney fee funding is requested, including anticipated court dates, negotiation timelines, litigation schedules, or other relevant timeframes.
3.	A detailed cost breakdown, including services to be provided, estimated attorney hours, hourly rates, and total costs. Requests must also include a tribal resolution, copies of legal counsel contracts, and a current comprehensive financial income statement demonstrating whether the tribe can pay all or part of the legal costs.
4.	A Regional Solicitor’s opinion regarding the tribe’s request.
5.	A certificate or statement from the attorney’s bar association confirming the attorney is a member in good standing.
6.	A memorandum from the Regional Director endorsing the tribe’s request for Attorney Fees/Litigation Support funding.
Agency and regional office program staff must review each request and provide recommendations and supporting information to assist the Attorney Fee Review Committee in determining an appropriate funding amount.

overview.objective: To implement those provisions of the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act of 1974, as amended, which are assigned to the Department of the Interior; and to institute conservation practices and methods to restore the grazing potential of rangelands lying within the former Navajo/Hopi Joint Use Area.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Implements the Department of the Interior's responsibilities under the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act by supporting settlement-related activities and restoring the grazing potential of rangelands within the former Navajo-Hopi Joint Use Area through conservation and sustainable land management practices, consistent with applicable federal laws and tribal self-determination authorities.

list.description: The Navajo-Hopi Settlement Program implements the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act of 1974, enhancing the BIA's mission by managing, protecting, and preserving agricultural and rangeland resources on Navajo and Hopi Partitioned Lands. Through BIA staff and Pub.L. 93-638 contracting, the program supports tribes and Indian farmers/ranchers by providing agricultural and range management assistance, including soil surveys, rangeland inventories, and land-use evaluations to inform planning and decision-making. It collaborates with tribal officials to identify rangeland infrastructure needs and implements improvements, maintaining livestock water developments, fencing, and pest control measures while managing invasive species and trespass livestock. Additionally, the program offers expertise for monitoring tribal self-determination contracts, ensuring compliance through on-site visits and technical assistance to address identified weaknesses.

title: Safety of Dams on Indian Lands

overview.objective: To improve the structural integrity of dams on Indian lands, including operations and maintenance of these dams.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Bureau of Indian Affairs’ (BIA) Safety of Dams (SOD) Program was established under the Indian Dams Safety Act (IDSA) of 1994, P.L. No. 103-302, 25 U.S.C. § 3801 et seq. SOD’s principal authorities include, but are not limited to, 25 U.S.C. §§ 3801 – 3805, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Federal Guidelines for Dam Safety.

The mission of SOD is to reduce the potential loss of human life and property damage caused by dam failure by making dams under the administration of the BIA as safe as practically possible. SOD endeavors to ensure that its dams are maintained in satisfactory condition on a long-term basis and to promote awareness and access to the beneficial uses achieved through public investments in SOD dam infrastructure.

When applicable, SOD program funds are awarded through Federal Acquisitions Regulation contracts.

overview.objective: The BIA Tribal GLRI Program offers financial support to Great Lakes Tribes, enabling them to carry out a wide range of projects aimed at protecting, enhancing, and restoring the Great Lakes ecosystem. Through this program, Tribes receive resources to help address environmental challenges affecting their communities and the natural surroundings they rely on. Priority actions under the program include identifying at-risk species and habitats, implementing strategies to protect and conserve these ecological assets, and managing ongoing restoration efforts that promote the health and sustainability of native wildlife and plant populations. In addition, the program emphasizes the importance of strengthening tribal capacity for natural resource management within the Great Lakes basin. This includes supporting activities such as training tribal staff, developing management plans, acquiring necessary tools and technology, and fostering collaboration with other organizations and agencies.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Tribal Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) has helped strengthen the ability of Tribal Nations to take part in shared decision making about Great Lakes resources. This support ensures that Tribes have the tools, funding, and opportunities needed to participate meaningfully when governments work together to manage and protect the basin. GLRI investments have also expanded community education and awareness, helping Tribal Nations share cultural teachings, subsistence practices, and traditional knowledge with Tribal youth and neighboring communities. The program provides dedicated funding for Tribal Nations to carry out their own priorities for restoring and protecting the Great Lakes. Tribes can implement projects that safeguard important species, strengthen Tribal lifeways, and uphold treaty reserved rights. The program supports a true government to government relationship, giving Tribes the flexibility to design and lead projects that best serve their communities and their lands. The program supports both Tribal capacity and on the ground restoration work. It funds the staff, training, and resources needed for long-term Tribal environmental programs, while also supporting projects that restore habitats, improve water quality, and protect species that are central to Tribal culture. This approach ensures that Tribal Nations are equipped not only to respond to today’s environmental challenges but also to maintain their stewardship roles for future generations. The program continues to advance Tribal led stewardship, protect important resources, and support the health of the Great Lakes for generations to come.

•	Habitat and fish and wildlife species protection, restoration, and enhancement, including removing barriers to fish passage and targeted protection and restoration of native and endangered species and their habitats in the Great Lakes
•	Foundations for future restoration actions, incorporating climate resiliency, education, and adaptive management to enhance accountability and provide science-based decision making to assess the overall health of the Great Lakes ecosystem and target significant remaining problems

overview.objective:
The Office of Native Hawaiian Relations’ (ONHR) Heritage (Tourism) Opportunities in Hawaiʻi (HŌʻIHI) Grant Program serves to implement the provisions of the Native American Tourism and Improving Visitor Experience Act (NATIVE Act), 25 U.S.C. 4351 et seq.  The purpose of the NATIVE Act is to establish a more inclusive national travel and tourism strategy that has the potential to deliver significant benefits for Native Hawaiian organizations (NHO) as distinctly defined in the NATIVE Act, including job creation, elevated living standards, and expanded economic opportunities.  

The HŌʻIHI Grant Program is an innovative effort to promote heritage tourism opportunities that utilize Native Hawaiian traditional knowledge to bolster economic development in the Native Hawaiian Community, to advance economic growth in the State of Hawaiʻi, and to equip Native Hawaiian organizations (NHO) with the needed resources to transform tourism involving historical and sacred sites to be regenerative and collaborative.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The HŌʻIHI Grant Program is an innovative initiative aimed at leveraging Hawaiian traditional knowledge to support economic development within the NHC, promote economic growth in Hawaiʻi, and provide Native Hawaiian organizations (NHO) with the needed resources to transform tourism into a regenerative and collaborative industry. Through the HOIHI Grant Program, NHOs lead the way in creating authentic experiences that reflect their values, knowledge, and practices, ensuring that cultural traditions are honored and transmitted in ways that are meaningful to the Community itself. By restoring decision-making regarding hoʻokipa (hospitality) practices to the Native Hawaiian Community, this program fosters a future where tourism serves as a platform for integrity and self-determination, rather than simply commodification.

The HŌʻIHI Grant Program additionally seeks to increase economic development within the NHC by expanding opportunities for entrepreneurship among members, increasing innovation potential on the usage and incorporation of traditional knowledge, and ultimately increasing growth of new businesses within the Community. This, in turn, broadens the ability of Native businesses to flourish and contribute to lowering unemployment and expanding economic growth.

ONHR will fulfill the core principles of the HŌʻIHI Program by providing grant funding to successful NHO applicants who meet the criteria for one or more of the following priorities:
1) Enhance the entrepreneurial capacity of the NHC by developing business opportunities in the visitor industry, providing business development training, or stimulating economic activity;
2) Uplift, perpetuate, and in some cases revive, traditional Hawaiian practices (e.g., ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi, kapa making, lauhala and kaula weaving, hula, amongst many others, including lesser-known practices) by creating opportunities for demonstrations, visitor education on history, usage, and protocols, or hands-on visitor participation experiences in the cultural practice;
3) Undertake related activities with visitors that convey respect and reaffirm the principle of reciprocation to the place, resources, and traditional knowledge holders and practitioners; AND/OR
4) Support the maintenance, enhancement, and protection of Hawaiʻi’s natural resources, wahi kūpuna (ancestral places), and wahi pana (sacred sites) at areas impacted by tourism while enhancing visitor services to promote respect and reciprocity.

assistanceUsage.description:
The American Rescue Plan provides financial assistance “for research and extension activities to strengthen early detection, rapid response, and science-based management to address wildlife disease outbreaks before they become pandemics and strengthen capacity for wildlife health monitoring to enhance early detection of diseases that have capacity to jump the species barrier and pose a risk in the United States.”  Funding will be used to establish and enhance Tribal, State, and Territorial fish and wildlife agencies’ capability to effectively address health issues involving free-ranging terrestrial, avian, and aquatic wildlife and minimize the negative impacts of health issues affecting free-ranging wildlife through surveillance, management, and research to protect the public against zoonotic disease outbreaks.  This new federal assistance program is designed to bring wildlife agencies to readiness against future pandemics and encourage them to coordinate their efforts regionally across state and Tribal boundaries. Assistance will be available for a range of activities with the goal of the program to strengthen the foundation of an interjurisdictional landscape-level wildlife health and disease network to protect wildlife, ecosystems, economies, and the American public. This goal is supported by the following objectives:
1.	Wildlife managers have a current, evidence-based wildlife disease plan which considers:   
a.	Disease surveillance and techniques for surveillance strategies   
b.	Diagnostic pathology, microbiology, virology, parasitology, toxicology procedures, and biosafety  
c.	Outbreak response  
d.	Host population management  
e.	Regulatory and policy response  
f.	Data management  
g.	Risk assessment and decision support  
h.	Training   
i.	Communication plans so that key entities receive and understand information about wildlife diseases in a timely manner. 
2.	State, territorial, and Tribal managers in the same regions are connected in an interjurisdictional network of practitioners.
3.	Wildlife managers have access to diagnostic services for wildlife disease.
4.	Wildlife managers have capacity to manage wildlife health data, data sharing, and communication.
Project length is one to three years. 
Applicants must fill out a survey at the beginning and end of their project. This survey is designed to evaluate the ARP ZDI financial assistance program and will not be used to evaluate individual proposals.

selectionCriteria.description:
Selection will be based on the merits of the proposal. Proposals must explain how the applicant will build an interjurisdictional landscape-level wildlife health and disease network to protect wildlife, ecosystems, economies, and the American public. Selection factors will be rated numerically and are as follows: Wildlife health management plan-10, Communications-10, Diagnostic access-10, Diagnostic access-10, Jurisdictions, authorities, and policies-10, Data and information management-10, Wildlife health capacity building-10, Training offered-10, Human dimensions-10, Occupational and public health-10, One Health concepts, including zoonotic disease prevention and management, are integrated throughout the proposal-2, Proposal has scientific merit, peer reviewed references provided-1, Clear writing, organized proposal-1, Methods and funding requested are commensurate with the proposed objectives-1, Innovative proposal and actions can be replicated elsewhere-1, Hiring practices or access to services show diversity, equity, and inclusion-1.
Proposal narratives must be 10 pages or less. Proposals will be rated by numeric score by qualified reviewers. Reviewers will be Federal veterinarians, biologists, ecologists, or social scientists or data management specialists. Qualifications will be verified by General Schedule professional qualifications. Selections will be documented by aggregated scoring sheets and memorandum to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director, filed in Science Applications Headquarters office. Proposals will be scored individually by 3 reviewers per proposal. All reviewers will be required to verify they have no conflict of interest with any proposal or applicant organization. Scores will be aggregated by the selection facilitator/grant specialist and then a meeting held to discuss scoring and to rank proposals. If reviewers have feedback or questions for applicants, grant specialist will communicate with applicants to suggest improvements or budget changes for approved projects. Unfunded projects will be notified through GrantSolutions (www.grantsolutions.gov). All project selections will be approved by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director or designate. Selected proposals will be published on our website no more than 120 days from proposal due date.

title: Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native Culture and Arts Development

overview.objective: The Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native culture and arts development program promotes the scholarly study of, and instruction in, Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native arts and culture; establishes programs which culminate in the awarding of degrees in the various fields of Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native art and culture; and establishes centers and programs with respect to Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native art and culture.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Secretary of the Interior is authorized to provide grants to private, nonprofit organizations or institutions that primarily serve and represent Native Hawaiians or Alaska Natives. To be eligible, these entities must be recognized by the Governor of Hawaii or Alaska for this purpose. The grants aim to support programs that preserve, revitalize, and develop Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native culture and arts, encompassing traditional and contemporary expressions in areas such as language, history, visual and performing arts, and crafts.

list.description: Funding from this program supports various initiatives aimed at promoting and preserving indigenous arts and culture. For example, one project recruits young adults interested in pursuing arts career pathways. These participants complete a pre-apprenticeship program in arts carving, followed by a mentor-apprentice program where they carve a totem pole under the guidance of a master carver. This project not only provides hands-on training but also academic credits towards a degree with an emphasis on arts. Another initiative focuses on revitalizing endangered cultural practices related to mountain goats, enhancing cultural practices, increasing community engagement, and passing down traditional skills to future generations. Additionally, the program supports the development and training of arts, offering instructional opportunities, collaborative academic offerings, and overall enrichment of arts for students and the general public.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that preserve, revitalize, and develop Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native culture and arts, encompassing traditional and contemporary expressions in areas such as language, history, visual and performing arts, and crafts.

overview.objective: Section 40904(b) of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, also known as the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, authorized the Secretary of the Interior to fund the rehabilitation, reconstruction, or replacement of a dam in which construction began on or after January 1, 1905, developed pursuant to the Carey Act (43 U.S.C. 641). To be eligible for funding, the Governor of the State in which the dam is located must determine that the dam has reached its useful life and poses significant health and safety concerns; and request Federal support. overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Snow Water Supply Forecasting listing provides assistance to improve water supply forecasting in snow‑driven river systems. Its goal is to enhance decision‑making by delivering more accurate, timely predictions of spring runoff. By advancing current monitoring methods, especially through emerging technologies, this program equips water managers with critical data, helping communities prepare for droughts, manage reservoir operations, and optimize water use. The listing serves a wide range of partners, including tribal nations, state and local governments, federal agencies, universities, irrigation and water districts, nonprofits, and private companies. By prioritizing operational relevance and measurable outcomes, the listing fosters partnerships that bridge research, technology, and real-world water management.

overview.objective: The objective of the Bureau of Land Management’s Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) for Recreation is to improve public access, visitor experiences, and recreation infrastructure on and near BLM-managed lands through partnerships with states, counties, and federally recognized Indian Tribes. This assistance listing supports cross-boundary recreation enhancement and improvement projects that increase the efficiency of project delivery, leverage partner capacity, and address shared recreation needs across jurisdictional boundaries. Eligible projects focus on planning, constructing, repairing, restoring, improving, or relocating recreation facilities and access infrastructure that benefit public use and recreation outcomes on BLM-managed lands and surrounding communities. Key objectives include expanding recreational access, enhancing visitor safety and amenities, or improving connections to existing recreation.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Bureau of Land Management’s Good Neighbor Authority for Recreation supports partnerships with states, counties, and federally recognized Indian Tribes to carry out recreation enhancement and improvement projects that expand and enhance public recreation opportunities on and near BLM-managed lands. This assistance listing provides a flexible, collaborative approach to improving recreation access and visitor infrastructure, including trails, trailheads, campgrounds, day-use areas, restrooms, parking areas, and other facilities that support public recreation. Projects may be implemented on Federal land, non-Federal land, or Tribal land when they enhance public access, visitor experiences, and recreation opportunities associated with BLM-managed lands and surrounding communities. Although an agreement may allow a cooperating entity to provide National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) services and site surveys, the decision to authorize a project remains the responsibility of the BLM and cannot be delegated.

financialInformation.additionalInformation:

This is a new authority for recreation, and no prior recreation assistance agreements have been executed under this listing. Accordingly, there are no prior-year obligations or reporting discrepancies associated with this Assistance Listing.

overview.objective: Provide funding to local governments with fire protection responsibilities to acquire slip-on tanker units to establish fleets of vehicles that can be quickly converted to be operated as fire engines.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The devastating intersection of extreme heat, drought, and wildland fire danger across the United States create wildfires that move with a speed and intensity previously unseen. This has created conditions in which wildfires overwhelm response capabilities, resulting in billions of dollars in economic losses, damage to natural resources, devastation to communities, and the tragic loss of human life. 

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, more commonly known as Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL), enacted in November 2021, is bringing much-needed support to communities across the country to increase the resilience of lands facing the threat of wildland fires and to better support federal wildland firefighter.  The BIL provides funding and authorizes the Department of the Interior (DOI) to develop and implement a pilot program to provide local governments financial assistance to acquire slip-on tanker units to establish fleets of vehicles that can be quickly converted to be operated as fire engines.

overview.objective:
This grant program is cooperatively administered by the U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Secretary, Interior Business Center, Acquisition Services Directorate (AQD) as part of the U.S. Government Interagency Agreement between the Office of Native Hawaiian Relations (ONHR) and AQD.  
The Kapapahuliau Grant Program, authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act (P.L. 117-169, Title VIII Sec. 80002), provides funding to Native Hawaiian Organizations to leverage traditional Native Hawaiian knowledge in enhancing response and resilience to adverse weather events and subsequent environmental impacts. The activities funded by this program aim to promote the self-sufficiency, self-determination, and self-reliance of the Native Hawaiian Community and their lands. Projects supported by the grant will address various issues such as drought, wildfires, invasive species, storm-related flooding, tidal inundation, and erosion mitigation, while also considering the associated economic impacts.  Kapapahuliau is centered around the following five Guiding Principles for which actions are carried out to support the overall Program Goal. Project proposals should look to meet all five of the following: 1)  Native Hawaiian Organizations currently represent the Native Hawaiian Community.  2) Aloha ʻĀina (love for the land): The Hawaiian Islands and its environment are essential to Native Hawaiian Community identity.  3) Severe weather and related environmental impacts inevitably cause economic hardship to the Native Hawaiian Community. 4) Native Hawaiian Community resilience must incorporate Native Hawaiian traditional knowledge systems and ingenuity.  5) Kuleana (Right & Responsibility) to advance Native Hawaiian Community resilience through dialog and shared learning.

overview.objective:
The U.S. Department of the Interior has been authorized by Congress to establish an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation (AHMR) Program under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA).  This program is separate and not inclusive of the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement’s (OSMRE) Abandoned Mine Lands Program.

Over the decades, extractive industry activities have left behind a number of underground and surface mines and features that pose physical safety hazards and have degraded the environment impacting local communities and created a loss of jobs in the mining industry.  

The program provides project grants to assist States, U.S. Territories, and Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments with mitigating the physical safety and contaminant risks associated with hardrock (non-coal) abandoned mine sites and features. The AHMR Program's outcomes include enhancing public safety and improving water, soil, and air quality by reducing or eliminating the physical safety of past hardrock mining activities on State, Tribal, and private lands.

list.description: To date, the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation (AHMR) Program provided more than $3.2 million in funding to States to inventory, assess, decommission, reclaim, respond to substance releases, and remediate abandoned hardrock mine lands so that lands may be returned to productive uses. Inventory projects will directly assist with gathering information regarding the location of mine sites on State and private lands that were abandoned to development of their originally targeted minerals, but may contain amounts of today's critical minerals, including in potentially easy-to-mine tailings piles. Seven financial assistance awards are for inventory only projects. Twelve financial assistance awards are for site projects to address health and safety risks associated with hardrock mining. Tribal consultation has been completed to advance the launch of the Tribal Grant Program.

In FY26, the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation (AHMR) Program has $4.9 million available in funding to eligible States and U.S. Territories to conduct the following activities: inventory, assess, decommission, reclaim, respond to substance releases, and remediate abandoned hardrock mine lands so that lands may be returned to productive uses. Inventory projects will directly assist with gathering information regarding the location of mine sites on State and private lands that were abandoned to development of their originally targeted minerals, but may contain amounts of today's critical minerals, including in potentially easy-to-mine tailings piles. Project work will include inventory and site projects to address health and safety risks associated with hardrock mining. 

In FY26, the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation (AHMR) Program has $1.8 million available in funding to eligible Federally recognized Indian Tribes to conduct the following activities: inventory, assess, decommission, reclaim, respond to substance releases, and remediate abandoned hardrock mine lands so that lands may be returned to productive uses. Inventory projects will directly assist with gathering information regarding the location of mine sites on Tribal lands that were abandoned to development of their originally targeted minerals, but may contain amounts of today's critical minerals, including in potentially easy-to-mine tailings piles. Project work will include inventory and site projects to address health and safety risks associated with hardrock mining. 

To date, two Federal Financial Assistance grant awards have been made to Federally registered Tribes and Alaskan Native Villages.

overview.objective: Under its Native American Business Development Institute (NABDI) conceived in FY 2006, IEED has developed partnerships with U.S. graduate schools to assist tribal business assess financial opportunities and prepare economic feasibility studies. Assistance by way of Public Law 93-638 agreements between tribes and participating business schools. During FY 2006- 2010, NABDI assisted tribes to analyze the potential of economic opportunities as diverse as a business park, a meat packing plant, a wind energy project, a security business, a medical supply business, upland bird hunting, new uses for a dormat tribal wellness/recreation center, and a greenhouse heated by way of woody biomass.  Starting in FY 2011, NABDI funding will be dispersed on a competitive basis following notice in the Federal Register.  Applicants will be free to choose private consultants in addition to graduate schools.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
Assistance Listing Number (ALN) 15.133, titled Native American Business Development Institute, is managed by the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Office of Indian Economic Development (OIED). Its primary purpose is to empower Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and their members by funding feasibility studies, market analysis, and business planning. These studies help tribes assess economic opportunities—such as business parks, meat processing operations, renewable energy ventures, security firms, and more—and determine whether they’re financially viable and sustainable.

NABDI stands out because it specifically supports economic feasibility research and business planning, rather than funding construction or direct business operations. From its start in fiscal year 2006, NABDI partnered with U.S. graduate schools and, later, private consultants, under Public Law 93‑638 agreements to assist tribal leaders in evaluating the financial and strategic aspects of projects. In doing so, it helps tribes produce investor‑quality business plans and feasibility reports that are essential for securing funding and attracting partners.

Only Federally Recognized Indian Tribes and Tribal Organizations are eligible to apply, and both they and their tribal members benefit from the insights and planning support these grants provide. Funding is awarded competitively and with the amount and number of awards depending on federal appropriations and the quality of proposals.

What makes NABDI unique is its focus on strategic preparation rather than immediate implementation. By financing deep-dive market and technical studies, NABDI reduces risk for tribes and helps them make informed, confident decisions. Furthermore, this grant program encourages tribes to engage consultants and graduate institutions, bringing professional rigor and external validation to their economic initiatives.

By helping tribes build solid, research-backed business cases, NABDI strengthens tribal sovereignty and economic independence. It allows communities to move forward with ventures grounded in rigorous analysis rather than guesswork—ultimately fostering sustainable job creation, enhanced revenues, and broader community development throughout Indian Country.

overview.objective: To provide development grants to Indian tribes for use in developing and sustaining the managerial and technical capacity needed to develop their energy resources, and to properly account for resulting energy production and revenues.  Proposals from tribes should strive to achieve the following stated goals: Evaluated the type and range of energy development activities that a tribe way want to assume under a TERA; Determine the current level of scientific, technical, administrative, for financial management capacity of the tribe to assume responsibility for the identified development activities; and determine which scientific, technical, administrative, or financial management capacities need enhancement and what process and/or procedures the grantee may use to eliminate these capacity gaps.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Tribal Energy Development Capacity (TEDC) grant provides Federally recognized Tribal entities and Tribal Energy Development Organizations with financial assistance to help them build the management, organizational, legal, and technical capacity needed to plan, regulate, and advance energy resource development on Tribal lands. TEDC supports Tribes in strengthening the foundational structures required to successfully manage energy projects, from establishing business entities and utility authorities to developing or updating Tribal laws, codes, and regulatory systems that govern energy development. The program also assists Tribes in creating the legal frameworks needed for business formation, land leasing for energy purposes, and secured transactions, as well as forming Tribal Energy Development Organizations. 

TEDC is unique because it focuses specifically on the capacity-building elements that must be in place before energy projects can move toward financing or construction. Rather than funding physical infrastructure, the program invests in the policies, institutions, and governance tools that enable Tribes to pursue energy development in alignment with Tribal goals. TEDC can also be used to support Tribes interested in advancing toward a Tribal Energy Resource Agreement.

By supporting early-stage planning and governance development, TEDC empowers Tribes to fully evaluate opportunities, reduce project risk, strengthen self-determination, and position their communities for long-term economic benefits from responsible energy development.

list.description: A Tribe was awarded funding to determine the feasibility of establishing a Tribal Utility Authority (TUA) aimed at increasing energy sovereignty and reducing reliance on external utilities. The proposed initiative responds to persistent challenges faced by the Tribe, including frequent power outages, dependence on external energy providers, and the vulnerability created by their remote location. These issues impact essential services and community safety, making local energy control a critical priority.

Tribal energy resource agreement readiness assessment, tribal energy development organization formation, business and legal planning for energy systems, tribal utility authority feasibility study, energy governance structure feasibility study, organizational review analysis

Needs to be met: To (1) leverage and expand assistance to single families and veterans, (2) address the dilapidated and overcrowded housing conditions in the Tribes’ service areas, (3) collaborate with other Federal housing programs to increase home ownership, repair and rehabilitation opportunities and develop strategies for increased energy efficiency and sustainability of new housing on Indian lands; and (4) increase the number of families assisted overall. 

Activities/projects to be conducted: Tiwahe Housing funding should be used in a matter more consistent with the Initiative and portions of their Tiwahe Housing funds may used in combination with other resources identified in each Tribe’s Tiwahe plan in the following areas: 
•	Foster care:  a system in which a minor has been placed into a ward, group home, or private home of a certified caregiver, referred to as a "foster parent".  The placement of the child is normally arranged through the government or a social service agency.
•	Transitional Housing: Housing with a time limit on how long you can stay in the housing or receive the housing assistance.  Housing and Urban Development (HUD) defines transitional housing as stays of up to twenty-four months (but stays can be shorter).
•	Short-Term or Temporary Housing:  Situations in which the housing situation is intended to be very short-term or temporary (thirty, sixty, or ninety days or less).
•	Emergency Shelter: to provide a place to stay or bed to sleep in overnight if you become homeless or otherwise experience a housing crisis and have no place to go.

*Restrictions: No new construction. Tiwahe housing funds support renovations. 
*No discretionary funds.
*No loan assistance applicable.
