title: Migratory Bird Monitoring, Assessment and Conservation

overview.objective: Working with others to conserve, enhance, and better understand the ecology and habitats of migratory bird species.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Migratory Bird Monitoring, Assessment and Conservation assistance listing provides financial and technical support to improve the science, management, and long‑term conservation of migratory birds across the United States. This program serves federal, state, Tribal, territorial, and local natural resource agencies; nonprofit organizations; research institutions; and other partners dedicated to understanding and sustaining healthy bird populations. 

 

At its core, the program invests in high‑quality monitoring, research, assessments, and decision‑support tools that help resource managers identify population trends, address emerging conservation challenges, and evaluate the effectiveness of habitat management actions. Projects may include population and habitat monitoring, evaluation of conservation strategies, development of analytical methods, and studies addressing the ecological needs of priority migratory bird species and the landscapes they depend on. 

 

What makes this assistance unique is its focus on science‑based management and the integration of biological monitoring with applied conservation action. By supporting projects that combine rigorous data collection, analysis, and communication, the program helps ensure that agencies and partners use the best available information when making conservation decisions. The listing also plays an important role in supporting cross‑agency collaboration, especially when migratory birds are affected by broader land management, climate, or ecosystem‑level changes. 

 

Recipients use assistance under this listing to improve understanding of bird population dynamics, evaluate how natural or human‑caused environmental changes may affect species, and design or refine conservation strategies that sustain migratory birds for the long term. Ultimately, the program supports transparent, high‑quality science that benefits the public by informing responsible stewardship of the nation’s migratory bird resources.

list.description: Shrub Removal for Training and Habitat: Invasive shrubs like buckthorn and honeysuckle are spreading rapidly at Fort Drum, creating dense thickets that block military training and reduce habitat quality for native wildlife. These shrubs may also contribute to the decline of the Golden-winged Warbler, a high‑priority conservation species with low nesting success on the installation. This project will test targeted mechanical and chemical treatments to remove invasive shrubs and improve both troop maneuverability and bird habitat. It will also study how shrub removal affects warbler nesting success, food availability, predation risk, and the broader bird community. Advanced remote‑sensing tools, including high‑resolution LiDAR and satellite imagery, will help map invasive plants and guide effective land management.

Managing Fire and Terrain for Eastern Black Rail Recovery: William & Mary’s Center for Conservation Biology will study how fire history, hydrologic restoration features, and small‑scale elevation changes affect Eastern Black Rail habitat use in South Florida. The project will survey sites across Everglades National Park, Big Cypress National Preserve, and nearby state lands to identify conditions that support this federally listed species. Results will provide managers with practical guidance on prescribed fire timing, placement of sheet‑flow features, and use of topographic diversity to maintain or improve habitat suitability. Deliverables include annual reports, a final management report, datasets, and a peer‑reviewed publication.

assistanceUsage.description: Grants and payments may be used for the conservation of any bird species protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Special emphasis will be placed on bird species listed in USFWS conservation and management priorities documents (e.g. USFWS Birds of Conservation Concern 2008, Focal Species list). Implementing national, regional, flyway Bird Conservation Region, and state-level bird conservation plans (e.g., Partners in Flight North American Landbird Conservation (http://www.partnersinflight.org), U.S. Shorebird Conservation Plan (https://www.fws.gov/birds/management/bird-management-plans/the-us-shorebird-conservation-plan.php) North American Waterbird Conservation Plan (https://www.fws.gov/birds/management/bird-management-plans/waterbird-conservation-for-the-americas.php) are among the Service's highest priorities. Projects related to the priorities identified in these plans will receive the greatest funding consideration. Projects should address one or more of the following activities: a) Population surveys and monitoring to determine the health, status, trends, and distribution of bird species and groups of concern. Emphasis will be placed on landscape-level applications of standardized inventory and monitoring protocols (e.g., Breeding Bird Atlases, national marshbird call playblack surveys). Local-scale monitoring (e.g., local land management units) activities will generally not be a focus of this program; b) Applied research, including but not limited to, studies of habitat requirements, limiting factors, and population responses to habitat conservation activities; development of new monitoring techniques and programs for poorly-surveyed species; use of Geographic Information Systems, bird habitat modeling, and similar tools to identify bird habitat focus areas and further bird conservation planning efforts; and investigation of avian mortality events and monitoring of health and disease problems; c) Compilation of technical information, such as status reviews of bird species of concern, development of habitat management and restoration guidelines, disseminating updates and providing training about current and emerging diseases which impact migratory bird populations, and other outreach and education programs including programs structured towards youth and connecting people with nature. Habitat management projects are generally not covered under this program. Additionally, construction or real property acquisition projects may not be funded under this program. For further information, please contact the regional office. Approximately 15% of program funding may be discretionary depending on annual appropriations and program priorities.

overview.objective: The purpose of the Natural Resource Damage Assessment and Restoration (NRDAR) Program is to restore natural resources and their services that have been injured by an oil spill or hazardous substance release for the benefit of the American people. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is a trustee for threatened and endangered species, migratory birds, at-risk species, and interjurisdictional fishes. We identify natural resources and their services that have been injured, determine the extent of the injuries, recover damages from responsible parties, and plan and carry out natural resource restoration activities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The purpose of the Natural Resource Damage Assessment and Restoration (NRDAR) Program is to restore natural resources and their services that have been injured by an oil spill or hazardous substance release for the benefit of the American people. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is a trustee for threatened and endangered species, migratory birds, at-risk species, and interjurisdictional fishes. We identify natural resources and their services that have been injured, determine the extent of the injuries, recover damages from responsible parties, and plan and carry out natural resource restoration activities.  

 

Assistance is provided to fund NRDAR-related activities that fall under two main sub-activities: 1) assessment, and 2) restoration. Assessment activities are funded from either appropriated funds or recovered past assessment costs. While assessment funding is discretionary, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other DOI Bureaus involved in NRDAR cases work as collaboratively as possible with our co-Trustees (e.g., states, federally-recognized tribes, and other federal agencies with natural resource management responsibilities that were impacted by the specific NRDAR case) when deciding what assessment activities to conduct and when to offer financial assistance for specific assessment activities. Assessment activities support the specific NRDAR case and legal claim, and can include identifying the natural resources injured and any loss of services they provide (such as recreation), determining the extent of the injuries, scaling restoration costs and projects to the injuries, and determining damages (i.e., cost) necessary to restore the injured natural resources and services. Restoration activities are funded from NRDAR case-specific settlement funds that were paid by the responsible party (or parties) to all Natural Resource Trustees that were part of the NRDAR claim. These funds are non-discretionary as their use is dictated by the court consent decree (CD) or the court-lodged settlement for the case. Furthermore, all Natural Resource Trustees must unanimously approve the expenditure of case settlement funds on restoration activities, through the administrative body of a Trustee Council (TC) and a TC Resolution. Additionally, the TC produces a restoration plan(s), which is publicly reviewed, that further directs how settlement funds are to be spent and the type of restoration projects and activities that can be conducted. Again, this restoration plan(s) involves the unanimous approval of all TC members before it can be finalized and implemented. Restoration activities are intended to restore, replace, or acquire the equivalent of the injured natural resources and their services. They can include the planning, implementation, and monitoring of restoration projects; the acquisition of land (for replacement of habitat, the benefit of injured wildlife species, and the benefit of the public); the creation of habitat, such as aquatic habitat in a stream or lake; and the creation, improvement, or enhancement of natural resource services, such as boating, hiking, and fishing opportunities, to replace lost services. All assistance provided for NRDAR activities, both assessment and restoration, must meet the intent of the NRDAR Program as well as the specific needs of a given NRDAR case.

list.description:
Collecting baseline information to restore northern gannet populations in north America, Gulf Restoration: To prepare for future on-the-ground restoration work identified in the Deepwater Horizon Natural Resource Damage Assessment Open Ocean Trustee Implementation Group Final Restoration Plan 3 and Environmental Assessment: Birds, we will collect baseline information on gannet populations at their colonies in 2024, including abundance, productivity, and disease status. This work is especially critical given uncertainties in how the population has responded to the major HPAI die-off event. Without such baseline information, effective restoration activities in future years would not be possible to implement, nor would responses to those activities be measurable. Specifically, we will conduct aerial surveys and ground monitoring at gannet colonies including swabbing gannets for HPAI and assessing any ongoing mortality to determine how/if HPAI is affecting colonies. In addition, we will control predators on colonies if detected during monitoring, as predator disturbance can have a major impact on colony abundance and productivity (i.e., would affect our ability to obtain baseline data). 

 

California seabird restoration and monitoring, CA: The California Seabird Restoration and Monitoring project aims to restore seabird nesting populations, particularly those of the common murre (Uria aalge), along the central California coast. Common murres and other seabird populations have been damaged by oil spills, gill-net fishing, and human disturbance. In 1953, the S.S. Jacob Luckenbach collided with the freighter Hawaiian Pilot and sank in waters approximately 27 kilometers southwest of San Francisco. Between 1990 and 2003, oil leaking from the sunken ship killed an estimated 51,569 seabirds, including 31,806 common murres. This project seeks to restore lost seabirds by reducing disturbance to colonies, thereby increasing reproduction. Methods including monitoring and surveillance to identify disturbance sources combined with outreach and education programs to pilots, boaters and other groups. 

 

Telogia creek water quality improvement project, GA: The Telogia Creek Water Quality Improvement project will reduce water quality degradation within Telogia Creek subbasin through a combination of GIS data analysis and implementation of site-specific restoration activities. The purpose of the project is to improve water quality by reducing sediment, nutrient, and pollutant loading and improving habitat stability and natural flow regimes. State of Florida water quality assessment within the Telogia Creek subbasin indicated that fecal coliform bacteria and dissolved oxygen are impairment concerns and nitrogen concentrations are increasing. Project goals are to improve surface water and aquatic habitat quality by implementing a variety of on-the-ground activities such as restoring eroding stream channels, establishing riparian buffers, improving unpaved road crossings, and restoring hydrologic connectivity. These restoration activities will reduce non-point source inputs into the system and diminish threats such as habitat and water quality degradation. Ultimately, the project will benefit freshwater resources, including Federally listed aquatic species, within the lower Ochlockonee River and estuarine and marine resources within the larger Ochlockonee Bay watershed. 

 

Allegan city dam removal data collection for sediment removal and channel restoration design work plan, MI: Allegan City Dam Sediment Characterization, MI: The Sediment Characterization at Allegan City Dam Projects aims to collect and analyze sediment samples upstream of the dam to pre-dam historic riverbed levels. The goal of the Allegan City Dam Characterization Project is to determine concentration of PCB-laden sediment above the dam to inform whether sediments can mobilize downstream or will require active management during dam removal. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, on behalf of the Trustee Council for the Kalamazoo River, acquired assessment funding for the project which will be carried out by Michigan’s Department for Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), a co-Trustee on the Kalamazoo Case. Funding was awarded in FY24 and work, including analysis of sediment, is expected to be completed by the end of FY25. 

 

Onondaga lake watershed open space land acquisition proposal: conservation in an increasingly developed basin, NY: The Wetland Trust proposal includes the acquisition and stewardship of approximately 275 acres for habitat preservation within the Onondaga Lake watershed. This project addresses the preferred restoration alternative of land preservation as described in the 2017 Onondaga Lake Natural Resource Damage Assessment Restoration Plan and Environmental Assessment. Expected outcomes of the acquisition and stewardship project include: 1) preservation of natural areas and restoration of habitats.

While assessment funding is discretionary, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other DOI Bureaus involved in NRDAR cases work as collaboratively as possible with our co-Trustees (e.g., states, federally-recognized tribes, and other federal agencies with natural resource management responsibilities that were impacted by the specific NRDAR case) when deciding what assessment activities to conduct and when to offer financial assistance for specific assessment activities.  Assessment activities support the specific NRDAR case and legal claim, and can include identifying the natural resources injured and any loss of services they provide (such as recreation), determining the extent of the injuries, scaling restoration costs and projects to the injuries, and determining damages (i.e., cost) necessary to restore the injured natural resources and services.

popularLongName: Great Lakes Restoration Initiative; Great Lakes Restoration Program

overview.objective: The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) provides environmental and public health benefits to the region’s twenty million Americans who rely on the Great Lakes for drinking water, recreation, and fishing. GLRI also fuels local and regional economies across the basin. Technical and financial assistance are provided in five focus areas: Toxic Substances and Areas of Concern, Invasive Species, Nonpoint Source Pollution, Habitats and Species, and Foundations for Future Restoration Actions.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) is a multiagency program established under Section 118 of the Clean Water Act to protect, restore, and enhance the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Great Lakes ecosystem. Through interagency collaboration led by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and supported by federal partners including the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the GLRI directs resources toward habitat restoration, invasive species prevention and control, reduction of toxic substances and habitat impairments in Areas of Concern, and actions that protect public health and local economies across the Great Lakes Basin. 

 

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) uses GLRI funds to implement science-based conservation actions that recover native species, restore and connect habitats, address threats such as aquatic invasive species, and deliver measurable ecological improvements identified in GLRI Action Plans. These activities are aligned with the Service’s mission and longstanding partnerships across the Basin and support broader federal priorities under the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. 

 

Assistance is provided primarily through cooperative agreements, interagency agreements, and other financial assistance instruments to Tribes, states, local governments, conservation organizations, academic institutions, and other partners engaged in protecting and restoring Great Lakes natural resources. Projects funded under this program advance locally led conservation, strengthen community resilience, and contribute to long-term recovery of fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats across the eight Great Lakes states.

list.description: Funded activities directly address the goals and objectives identified in the GLRI Action Plan IV (https://www.glri.us) and include restoration, protection and enhancement of coastal, terrestrial and wetland habitat for migratory birds and nearshore aquatic species; restoration of riverine habitats to improve aquatic habitat connectivity for fish and other aquatic organisms; prevention, early detection and control of invasive species such as invasive carp; restoration of native aquatic species, such as Lake Trout and Lake Sturgeon, to self-sustaining levels.

Projects anticipated to be funded include restoration, protection and enhancement of coastal, terrestrial and wetland habitat for migratory birds and nearshore aquatic species; restoration of riverine habitats to improve aquatic habitat connectivity for fish and other aquatic organisms; prevention, early detection and control of invasive species such as invasive carp; restoration of native aquatic species, such as Lake Trout and Lake Sturgeon, to self-sustaining levels

overview.objective: Partnering with individuals, government agencies, nonprofit organizations and corporations, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) works to protect and restore imperiled species, promote healthy oceans and estuaries, improve working landscapes for wildlife, advance sustainable fisheries and conserve water for wildlife and people. NFWF is an independent 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, governed by a 30-member Board of Directors approved by the Secretary of the Interior. Conservation programs cover many ecosystems and address challenges in oceans and coasts, forests and grasslands and freshwater environments. This program uses direct funding only from the annual appropriations law for on-the-ground conservation matched at least at a 1:1 basis.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The partnership between the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) is a cornerstone of American conservation, leveraging public funds with private funds to protect and enhance fish, wildlife, plants and their habitats. This partnership funds science-based, community-driven projects focusing on restoring ecosystems across all 50 states and territories. FWS provides critical base funding, which NFWF leverages to attract private sector dollars, creating a massive multiplier effect for conservation projects. Projects cover a vast array of areas to support imperiled species (turtles, birds, bats, fish) and working lands (farmers, ranchers) through targeted conservation projects.

overview.objective: Emergency Wetlands Resources Act - National Wetlands Inventory, 16 U.S.C. §3901 and §§3931-3932. The Emergency Wetlands Resource Act requires the National Wetlands Inventory Program (NWI) to map wetlands of the nation, digitize the maps, archive and distribute the data, and produce a 10-year national wetlands status and trends report to Congress.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The purpose of this listing is to enable the National Wetlands Inventory Program to work with cooperators to help meet its statutory requirements to provide information to the public on the extent and status of the nation’s wetland and deepwater habitats, as well as changes to these habitats over time. This information is available to the public through two resources: the Wetlands Geospatial Dataset and Wetlands Status and Trends reports. These provide complementary information on wetland and deepwater habitat type, location, and trends to support decision makers. The NWI dataset is unique in its national scope and standardization, enabling a wide variety of uses from watershed planning to streamlined permitting to energy development.

list.description: The National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) Program received two applications for new projects and two amendments for ongoing projects. The amendments increased the area of NWI wetlands geospatial data produced in the Prairie Pothole Region, Mississippi River Valley, and Virginia by approximately 760,000 acres. The new projects supported NWI wetland mapping in Pennsylvania and Alaska.
Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that will produce maps and geospatial data of American wetland and deepwater habitats.

overview.objective: To provide federal financial assistance to livestock producers undertaking proactive, non-lethal activities to reduce the risk of livestock loss due to predation by wolves and to compensate livestock producers for livestock losses due to such predation.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Wolf Livestock Loss Demonstration Project Grant Program, authorized through Subtitle C of the Omnibus Public Lands Management Act of 2009, provides federal financial assistance to states and tribes to assist livestock producers in undertaking proactive, nonlethal activities to reduce the risk of livestock loss due to predation by wolves and to reimburse livestock producers for livestock losses due to such predation.  Proactive, nonlethal preventive measures eligible for funding include, but are not limited to, fencing, livestock guard dogs, and range riders who patrol areas occupied by livestock susceptible to predation by wolves. Depredation compensation funding may be used for the reimbursement of livestock losses due to confirmed wolf depredation. Qualifying livestock includes cattle, swine, horses, mules, sheep, goats and livestock guard animals.

overview.objective: To conserve priority lands and natural resources and recognize the importance of the water, forest, agricultural, wildlife, recreational, and cultural resources, and the national significance of the Highlands region of the United States.  Preserve and protect high-priority conservation land in the Highland regions.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Highlands Conservation Act (H.R. 1964, 2004; 16 U.S.C. 3901) (HCA) authorizes a grant program in four States (Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania) to support State Agency land conservation priorities and protect natural resources in the Highlands Region, a nationally-important landscape distinguished by Appalachian ridges, hills, and plateaus that provides outdoor recreational opportunities for millions of people living in and visiting the Northeast. Conservation land acquired under the program may only be held by a State Conservation Agency, a County, or a Municipality within the designated Highlands Region. 

 

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is the lead agency for administering the HCA Grant Program, and works in partnership with State Conservation Agencies, the counties and municipalities of the Highlands Region, and the U.S. Forest Service. Since passage of the HCA in 2004, more than 20,000 acres of state-priority land have been conserved under the program. Projects support key conservation objectives outlined in the HCA such as protecting high priority water, forest, wildlife, agriculture, and recreational resources.

overview.objective: The Collaborative Landscape Conservation program promotes an inclusive approach to conservation by convening and facilitating diverse partnerships to address shared conservation challenges and create a network of healthy lands and waters where fish, wildlife, plants, and people thrive. The program advances adaptive leadership in landscape conservation regionally and nationally by identifying shared priorities with states, tribes, private landowners, academic institutions, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) coordinating actions, and informing decision-making. We support research to improve strategic conservation at the landscape scale, including development of data-driven decision support capability that make collaborative conservation achievable and support resilient landscape design which considers wildlife and ecosystems as well as cultural, social, and economic priorities. We support building collaborative conservation and the co-production of science by increasing capacity and support to effectively engage partners, synthesize information, and produce strategic approaches for landscape conservation.

overview.objective: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) uses a science-based, adaptive framework for setting and achieving broad-scale conservation objectives that strategically address the problems fish and wildlife will face in the future. This framework, called Strategic Habitat Conservation, is based on the principles of adaptive management and uses population and habitat data, ecological models, and focused monitoring and assessment efforts to develop and implement strategies that result in measurable fish and wildlife population outcomes. This process uses the best available scientific information to predict how fish and wildlife populations will respond to changes in the environment, thus enabling the USFWS to focus habitat conservation and other management activities where they will be most effective.   In addition, the USFWS needs focused, applied science directed at high impact questions surrounding threats to fish and wildlife resources for which management and/or mitigation is required to maintain species at healthy, sustainable, desired levels. USFWS must base its decisions on the best science available, in order to defend its regulatory decisions, biological opinions and species conservation recommendations to land managers.

list.description: Satellite remote sensing underpins conservation planning in the SCD. Building on existing rangeland products and collaborating with USDA ARS and the RAP team, we aim to develop next-generation models to detect and assess invasive annual grass (IAG) dynamics across the sagebrush biome. Because IAGs drive 55–70% of biome loss, this proposal focuses on improving their detection, though enhancements will also support monitoring of conifer expansion. Improved datasets will help practitioners better target treatments and evaluate their effectiveness at management scales. The primary objective is to research, develop, and test methods that advance satellite-based monitoring of invasive annual grasses.
Program anticipates funding projects that result in measurable fish and wildlife population outcomes.

title: Yukon River Salmon Research and Management Assistance

overview.objective: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service) receives funds for implementation of the Yukon River Salmon Agreement with Canada which was reached in March 2001.  The Yukon River Salmon Act of 2000 authorizes funds for implementation of the Agreement including funds for cooperative research and management projects on the Alaska portion of the Yukon River.  The Service administers these funds through financial assistance on a competitive basis for projects/studies that advance the scientific community’s understanding and management of Chinook and chum salmon in the Yukon River of Alaska.

overview.objective:
Support the implementation of the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy and assist at-risk communities from catastrophic wildfires, this initiative provides assistance in the following areas: development and enhancement of local programs focused on risk assessment, planning, training, mitigation activities, and community and homeowner education; planning and execution of fuels management reduction activities aimed at reducing the threat of catastrophic wildfires to communities and natural resources in high-risk areas, including associated monitoring and maintenance efforts on federal and adjacent non-federal land; increasing employment opportunities for local and small businesses in rural communities; and delivering education and training to improve the fire protection capabilities and knowledge of rural fire districts. Additionally, authorized restoration services under this section may be provided. All federal land within timber sale projects conducted under this authority shall be included. Projects that include a cost-sharing component or in-kind services will be prioritized for selection. Planning and implementation of fuels management reduction activities aimed at mitigating the threat of catastrophic wildfire to communities and natural resources in high risk areas, including associated monitoring or maintenance, on federal land and/or on adjacent nonfederal land; 
Enhancement of local and small business employment opportunities for rural communities; and providing education and training focused on increasing knowledge and fire protection capability of rural fire districts. Funding may also be allocated for wildland fire preparedness including wildfire prevention, detection, equipment, training, suppression, active wildfire response, and fire science and research. Additionally, funds may support hazardous fuel reduction and other fire-related activities such as site rehabilitation, assistance programs, research, and facilities maintenance.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: To provide federal financial assistance to secure information and undertake actions that will help prevent extinction and aid in recovery and delisting of Canis lupus baileyi. Funding is used to support various stages of reintroduction, monitoring, and management of southwest wolf populations in a manner that promotes viable ranching, self-sustaining and recovering wolf populations, and healthy western landscapes. Examples of funding include for states and tribes participating in on-the-ground wolf management, universities conducting critical analyses to support recovery, and zoological institutions conducting research and providing source populations for achieving recovery and a backstop to extinction.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Marine Mammal Protection Act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to carry out a grant program to provide financial assistance to rescue and respond to stranded marine mammals. Specifically, this program provides critical funding to entities that recover, care, and treat sick, injured, or entangled marine mammals; respond to marine mammal stranding events that require emergency assistance; and collect data and samples from living or dead stranded marine mammals for scientific research or assessments regarding marine mammal health. The grant program also supports facility operating costs and the development of stranding network capacity, including training for emergency response, where facilities do not exist or are sparse. The Prescott Grant Program has been very successful in providing vital funding to support polar bear, sea otter, walrus, and manatee rescue and rehabilitation efforts across the country.

The term “eligible marine mammal stranding participant” means a person who is authorized under MMPA section 104(c) for response to injured or distressed marine mammals or for scientific research regarding marine mammal health, or under MMPA section 112(c) to take marine mammals as described in MMPA section 109(h) in response to a stranding. To be eligible for Prescott Grants under this Funding Opportunity, such authorizations must have been issued by the FWS. Eligible entities also include Federal, state, or local government employees operating in the course of their official duties as indicated under MMPA section 109(h). overview.objective: The goal of White-nose Syndrome National Response Implementation is to conserve and recover bat species affected by the fungal disease white-nose syndrome (WNS) through partnership driven management, research and communication. WNS Grants to States and Tribes support agencies and organizations for management planning and actions, coordination of research activities, and collaboration with partners around conservation of hibernating bat species. WNS Research for Conservation Grants, if offered, provide support for research projects that address critical information needs for managing WNS and species affected by it. Grants and cooperative agreements support development and implementation of management tools and strategies to lessen the impacts of white-nose syndrome on hibernating bat species and conduct monitoring efforts to assess status and trends of North American bat populations.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The White-nose Syndrome National Response provides the framework for a broad partnership of government and non-government entities engaged in bat conservation and management. The partnership comprises federal, state, tribal, provincial agencies and non-government organizations and institutions across North America and beyond contributing to cross-border coordination, research, pathogen and disease surveillance, disease management, information sharing, and public engagement. A primary federal role is to provide funding for State wildlife management agencies to address bat conservation and WNS-related needs. 

 

WNS Grants to States and Tribes provide funding to wildlife agencies and departments conducting research and management of hibernating bat species. Funding through this opportunity supports local management of bats with cross-jurisdiction coordination to leverage efforts among partners. This grant program helps partners maintain staff dedicated to management of bats and supports their completion of projects that have lasting benefits to bat species and reduce the potential for federal regulatory action in the future. 

 

Cooperative agreements and WNS Research for Conservation Grants support high impact research needed to develop, test, inform and use management tools and disease treatments that improve survival of bats affected by WNS.

list.description: The Service provided awards through the WNS Grants to States and Tribes to support state agencies and tribes in their activities to manage WNS and bat species affected by it. Awarded funds are used by partners to implement and advance WNS treatments, conduct bat population monitoring, secure important bat roosts and maintain expertise engaging with the public, landowners, the WNS National Response Program and the North American Bat Monitoring Program. WNS Research for Conservation Grants supported projects to improve our knowledge about WNS progression and effects in western United States and to advance research on biotechnological tools to manage the fungal pathogen. These projects provide information to support management decisions and advance the administration’s priorities in support of energy and timber production and delivery.

The Service intends to provide awards through the WNS Grants to States and Tribes to support state agencies and tribes in their activities to manage WNS and bat species affected by it. Funds will be used to support partnership-driven management and monitoring activities. Funded work will include implementation and advancement of WNS treatments, conducting bat population monitoring, securing important bat roosts and maintaining expertise within the recipients’ organizations to effectively manage bats. Funds will also allow for recipients’ engagement with the WNS National Response Program and North American Bat Monitoring Program. WNS Research for Conservation Grants and cooperative agreements, if available, will support projects to improve our knowledge about WNS and susceptible bats to inform management decisions and advance the administration’s priorities for energy and timber production and delivery. Potential projects include investigation of physiological and behavioral mechanisms of resistance to WNS, testing and improvement of WNS treatments including biotechnological innovations, and adaptive management applications using WNS treatments in the field. The Service will also seek to support research and monitoring of bats on privately owned working forests and other important bat habitat.

overview.objective: To restore native fish and other aquatic species to self-sustaining levels by reconnecting habitat that barriers have fragmented, where such reconnection would not result in a net negative ecological effect such as providing increased habitat to aquatic nuisance species. Fish passage projects restore unimpeded flows and fish movement by removing barriers or providing ways for aquatic species to bypass them; such projects also provide public safety and economic benefits for human communities. The program works on a voluntary basis and provides financial support and technical assistance to Federal, State, local, and tribal agencies, as well as private partners and stakeholders.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The National Fish Passage Program (NFPP) is a voluntary cooperative conservation program administered by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS) that provides financial and technical assistance to reconnect aquatic habitats fragmented by barriers such as culverts and outdated infrastructure. Millions of aging barriers across the country fragment rivers, block fish migration, and increase flood risk to farms and communities. Removing them upgrades failing infrastructure, restores productive fishing waters, and expands public access for recreation, hunting, and fishing; all while benefiting farmers, rural communities, and local economies. 

 

What sets the NFPP apart is its cooperative, partnership-driven model. Rather than functioning as a traditional grant program, the USFWS works directly with partners to identify and fund the highest-priority projects, relying on a nationwide network of biologists and engineers at Fish and Wildlife Conservation Offices. Funding is open to federal and state agencies, Tribes, non-governmental organizations, ranchers, and private landowners for project types including culvert replacements, floodplain restoration, fishway installation, low-water crossings, bypass channels, water diversion modifications, and engineering and assessment work.

overview.objective:
The town of Nicodemus, in Kansas, has national significance as the only remaining western town established by African-Americans during the Reconstruction period following the Civil War. The town of Nicodemus is symbolic of the pioneer spirit of African-Americans who dared to leave the only region they had been familiar with to seek personal freedom and the opportunity to develop their talents and capabilities. 


The purposes of this program is to preserve, protect, and interpret for the benefit and enjoyment of present and future generations, the remaining structures and locations that represent the history (including the settlement and growth) of the town of Nicodemus, Kansas; and to interpret the historical role of the town of Nicodemus in the Reconstruction period in the context of the experience of westward expansion in the United States.

title: National Geospatial Program: Building The National Map

overview.objective: The National Map is a collaborative effort among the USGS and other Federal, State, Universities, and local partners to improve and deliver topographic information for the Nation.  The 3D National Topography Model, including the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) and the 3D Hydrography Program (3DHP), is an initiative that updates, improves, and integrates USGS elevation and hydrography data to support the most demanding scientific requirements and enable data-driven decisions across user communities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Geospatial Program provides opportunities for partnering with the USGS and other Federal agencies to acquire high-resolution 3D elevation and 3D hydrography data to support the 3D National Topography Model (3DNTM). The collaboration across the Nation responds to a growing need for high-quality elevation and hydrography data which benefit society in array of critically significant applications such as flood-risk management, natural-hazard evaluation and mitigation, and agriculture. The USGS
collaborates with State, Tribal, local, academic, and private sector partners to acquire data which are made publicly available and form the base of the elevation and hydrography components of The National Map.

list.description: The State of Michigan is working on a 3D Hydrography Program (3DHP) project to upgrade its surface water mapping, or hydrography, data, including information about rivers, streams, lakes, and other water features. This effort focuses on the western Upper Peninsula and the southwest Lower Peninsula. The project uses 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) Quality Level 2 lidar data and follows current U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) standards for 3DHP data. Multiple State agencies are collaborating to improve the accuracy and detail of Michigan’s water‑related maps and datasets. Once this project finishes, the remaining parts of the Upper Peninsula and the southwest Lower Peninsula will be complete, resulting in a fully updated, statewide 3DHP dataset. These improved data will also be included in the USGS National Geospatial Program’s National Map.

New York State is continuing its effort to update its elevation data using lidar technology through the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP). This project will gather new elevation data for parts of Allegany, Cattaraugus, Genesee, Livingston, Steuben, and Wyoming counties. The new data will replace older datasets and will meet current 3DEP quality standards. The project area overlaps with existing data to support review and accurate alignment of the new data. The project was selected following discussions with Federal Emergency Management Agency, U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service, and the U.S. Geological Survey to ensure it fits well with other ongoing mapping efforts. Planning has been completed with input and support from New York State agencies, counties, and regional organizations.

title: Volcano Hazards Program Research and Monitoring

overview.objective: To advance the scientific understanding of volcanic processes and to lessen the harmful impacts of volcanic activity. The Volcano Hazards Program (VHP) monitors active and potentially active volcanoes, assesses their hazards, responds to volcanic crises, and conducts research on how volcanoes work to fulfill a Congressional mandate (Public Law 93-288) that the USGS issue "timely warnings" of potential volcanic hazards to responsible emergency-management authorities and to the populace affected. VHP provides domestic assistance in order to expand the expertise and capabilities applied to fulfilling its mission.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Volcano Hazards Research and Monitoring Program supports long standing partnerships with state geological surveys and university collaborators that work with the five U.S. volcano observatories. These partners provide specialized scientific expertise and on the ground capabilities essential for monitoring and studying volcanic activity in Alaska, Hawaii, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming (Yellowstone). Their work generates critical data used by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) to meet its Congressional mandate to deliver timely and reliable warnings of potential volcanic hazards that threaten public safety.

This assistance strengthens the nation’s ability to understand, detect, and respond to volcanic unrest by ensuring that research, monitoring, and hazard assessments are informed by the best available science. It uniquely supports cooperative agreements with established regional experts whose long term knowledge of local volcanic systems contributes directly to national risk reduction efforts. The program also advances the goals of the National Volcano Early Warning and Monitoring System (Public Law 116 9) by prioritizing high threat volcanoes and sustaining the scientific partnerships needed to improve eruption forecasts, support emergency managers, and enhance community preparedness.

list.description: Continued funding of several long-standing cooperative agreements with state geological surveys and universities for supporting monitoring and mapping of U.S. volcanoes, and educating the public and decision-makers about volcanic hazards. FY25 funding will support development of new AVO website; response support for eruptions in Alaska and Hawaii; and continued seismic monitoring of volcanoes in Wyoming, and the Cascades Range

Program provides continued funding for several long-standing cooperative agreements with state geological surveys and universities for supporting monitoring and hazard assessments of U.S. volcanoes, educating the public and decision-makers about volcanic hazards, and supporting volcanic eruption response.

the effectiveness of potential management actions, enabling them to make informed, cost-effective decisions.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Office of Insular Affairs (OIA) carries out the Secretary’s responsibilities for U.S.-affiliated insular areas. These include the territories of American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI). Residents of these U.S. territories are U.S. citizens or U.S. nationals. Additionally, OIA administers and oversees Federal assistance to three freely associated states (FAS): the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), and the Republic of Palau (Palau). The territories are an integral part of the fabric of America, and the freely associated states, while independent countries, are uniquely interwoven with the United States in terms of a shared history, ongoing partnership, and a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific. Each of the territories and freely associated states are unique, yet their economies are all small, isolated, and dependent on one or two main sources of income. The Office of Insular Affairs has an important role to play in understanding the nuances of the Federal government’s interrelationship with each of the insular areas. OIA facilitates coordination of Federal policies and programs to best serve the insular areas and utilizes its own assistance programs to fill gaps not fulfilled by other Federal programs to meet the needs of the insular areas. OIA programs are purposely designed to offer the flexibility needed to respond to urgent, immediate needs in the insular areas.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) Grants provides funding to help museums, federally recognized Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations consult on, document, and return Native American human remains and cultural items with cultural significance. This program supports the repatriation process, covering activities like consultation, travel, transportation, contamination removal, reburial, storage, and related staff time.

list.description:
1) Repatriation and Return Activities - These projects focus on safely and respectfully returning ancestors or cultural items.

2) Consultation & Collaboration Projects - These projects help communities and institutions work together to plan returns and resolve cultural questions.

3) Documentation & Research Projects - These projects gather information needed to determine origin, cultural connection, or proper treatment.

4) Preparation and Care of Collections - These projects ensure items are properly handled before, during, or after consultation.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects to museums, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations to assist in consultation, documentation and repatriation under NAGPRA.

list.description: 1) Repatriation of Ancestral Remains: a museum successfully repatriated the remains of numerous ancestors and associated funerary objects to a Native American tribe. This project involved detailed consultations, updating inventories, and ensuring that cultural items were accurately identified and documented, facilitating future repatriation efforts. 3) Collaborative Projects: A tribal council worked with multiple museums to repatriate culturally significant items. These collaborative efforts ensured that items were returned to their rightful communities, where they could be reintegrated into cultural practices and ceremonies.

title: National Center for Preservation Technology and Training

overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports projects that develop innovative tools, materials, and methods for preserving historic buildings, landscapes, and cultural resources across the United States. The National Park Service’s National Center for Preservation Technology and Training (NCPTT) partners with public institutions, governments, and educational organizations to advance the field of preservation and make new technologies more accessible to practitioners and the public. What makes this program unique is its focus on innovation. Funded projects are expected to push the preservation field forward—developing new methods, adapting emerging technologies, or finding creative ways to share preservation knowledge widely.

list.description:
1) Research and Innovation - Projects include researchers studying how large technology facilities can be designed so they do not disrupt important community views and sounds, such as historic farms, old buildings, monuments, and outdoor art;  a team testing a new way to visualize and honor gravesites by creating digital models, helping families and communities remember and learn about them; and experts developing new imaging methods to help preserve historic photographic prints and plates by testing polarized and multispectral imaging techniques.

2) Technology Development - Projects include developers creating a mobile app that uses interactive storytelling and language technology to guide building owners and renters through the steps to check and repair historic buildings after a flood; and researchers creating an artificial‑intelligence‑based system that monitors how historic buildings are used so caretakers can better plan for their future.

3)  Digital Documentation and Visualization - Projects include a research team using drones to safely map the inside of old buildings that are too dangerous to enter, creating digital models that help experts understand structural conditions and plan preservation work.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that support innovative research and training projects that advance the practice of historic preservation. The goal is to fund cultural resource projects that will create better tools, better materials, and better approaches for protecting historic buildings and landscapes, and other significant cultural resources.

list.description:
1) Advancing Research That Protects Community Heritage - Researchers created new ways to design and operate high‑tech facilities so they do not harm the treasured views and soundscapes that matter to local communities. Their work helps protect scenic landscapes, historic farms, older buildings, monuments, outdoor sculptures, cemeteries, and historic battlefields.

2) Building Tools That Make Preservation Easier for the Public - A university team developed a user-friendly mobile app that guides building owners, renters, and managers through the steps to inspect and recover historic buildings after floods. The app uses interactive storytelling and language technology to make complex instructions simple and accessible.

3) Innovative Digital Documentation of Historic Places - Researchers used drones to safely map the interiors of historic structures that are too dangerous or unstable to enter. They produced detailed blueprints and digital models that help experts understand structural conditions and plan preservation work. Funding also supported early work on digital visualization techniques that allow families and communities to better understand and honor historic gravesites.

3) Improving Care for Historic Materials - Scientists tested new imaging methods to help preserve historic photographic prints and plates. By experimenting with polarized and multispectral imaging, they produced practical information that can help museums and archives protect important photographs for future generations.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that support innovative research and training projects that advance the practice of historic preservation. The goal is to fund cultural resource projects that will create better tools, better materials, and better approaches for protecting historic buildings and landscapes, and other significant cultural resources.

overview.objective: The National Maritime Heritage Grants Program provides matching grants for education and preservation projects designed to preserve historic maritime resources and to increase public awareness and appreciation for the maritime heritage of the United States. The grants will help State, Tribal, and local governments and private nonprofit organizations preserve and interpret their maritime heritage.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The National Maritime Heritage Grants provide 1-to-1 matching funds for a wide range of preservation and education projects in three broad categories: Historic Maritime Properties, Maritime Heritage Collections, and Traditional Maritime Skills. Grant projects are intended to help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.

list.description:
1) Education & Public Awareness: Funding may support projects that help people learn about the nation’s maritime past. This can include creating exhibits, programs, or community activities that explain how ships, waterways, and maritime travel shaped history. Grants may also help organizations develop workshops, teaching materials, or digital content that make maritime stories accessible to the public.

2) Preservation & Conservation: Funds may be used to protect and care for historic maritime resources. This could involve repairing or stabilizing vessels, artifacts, and archaeological collections, or performing engineering studies and scientific tests to understand their condition. Projects may focus on preserving materials so they can be safely exhibited, researched, or passed on to future generations.

3) Research & Documentation: Grants may support efforts to document and study maritime sites and collections. This includes researching underwater archaeological areas, examining historical records, and creating detailed documentation of artifacts or structures. These projects help deepen understanding and ensure accurate interpretation of maritime heritage.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Preserving Important Maritime History - Funding through this program has helped protect and conserve historic ships, maritime structures, and archaeological collections. Support has been used to carry out engineering studies, stabilize fragile materials, and complete conservation work so historic maritime resources can be safely preserved and shared with future generations. These efforts keep irreplaceable pieces of maritime history intact and accessible.

2) Expanding Public Access to Maritime Heritage - Awards have enabled public agencies and organizations to create exhibits, rehabilitate collections, and open more maritime materials for viewing, research, and education. By improving displays, enhancing storage and interpretation, and increasing access to coastal or underwater archaeological resources, the program helps the public better understand and appreciate the nation’s maritime past.

3) Supporting Community Learning and Education - The program has funded educational initiatives that bring maritime stories to communities across the country. These projects include developing teaching materials, creating public programs, and supporting cultural organizations in sharing the role of waterways, seafaring, and coastal industries in shaping national history.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.

overview.objective: To provide Federal financial assistance to State, local and tribal governments, other public entities, educational institutions, and private nonprofit organizations to identify, evaluate, interpret, and protect historic battlefields and sites associated with armed conflicts on American soil through non-acquisition projects and activities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The American Battlefield Protection Program offers grants to help protect, preserve, and interpret historic battlefield sites across the country. These grants serve state, tribal, and local governments, as well as universities and nonprofit organizations, helping them carry out non-land-acquisition projects that make battlefield history accessible and meaningful to the public.

list.description:
1) Studying and Mapping Historic Battlefields: Funding can support archaeological field surveys and research to locate battlefield features, map troop movements, and better understand how past conflicts unfolded. These projects help identify where fighting took place, uncover physical evidence, and document important aspects of battlefield history. 

2) Updating Battlefield Preservation Plans: Grants may be used to update long-term plans that guide how historic battlefields should be protected and cared for. This can include studying landscape changes, assessing threats, and planning how the site can be preserved for future generations.

3) Improving Battlefield Exhibits and Visitor Centers: Funding can help create new displays, update interpretive content, and install interactive exhibits that explain what happened during a battle. These improvements help visitors better understand troop actions, civilian experiences, and how the site played a role in major events.

4) Documenting Battlefield Heritage for Future Protection: Funding can support detailed documentation of battlefield history, including research into the people who fought there, the communities affected, and the broader military context. These efforts help ensure the site’s historical significance is clearly understood and preserved.

5) Restoring Battlefield Features and Historic Structures: Some funding helps stabilize or restore battlefield features—like earthworks, historic buildings, or defensive structures—to reflect their appearance at the time of conflict. This work protects fragile resources and allows the public to better visualize historic conditions.

This program helps people discover and learn from America’s historic battlefields by supporting projects that bring these places and the stories behind them to life. Funding is used to modernize how battlefield history is shared—through mobile apps, interactive websites, short films, and digital tools that make learning accessible to everyone, including those with limited hearing or vision. It also supports the digitization of historic documents, research into archaeological evidence, and hands‑on activities that allow students, veterans, and community members to participate directly in uncovering and interpreting the past.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: 1) Educational and Interpretive Projects: Funding was used to develop interactive exhibits and augmented reality applications at historical sites. These projects make history more engaging and accessible by allowing visitors to visualize historical events superimposed on the present landscape, enhancing their understanding and experience. 2) Archaeological Research and Field Investigations: Grants supported archaeological field investigations to uncover and document historical battlefields. This included conducting surveys, excavations, and using remote sensing technologies to better understand the events that took place and to preserve the sites for future generations. 3) Conservation and Restoration Projects:  Funding supported the physical conservation and restoration of historic sites and artifacts. This included stabilizing structures, repairing damage, and implementing measures to protect against future deterioration, ensuring these sites remain intact for future generations.

1) Revealing Hidden Battlefield History - Many projects have completed archaeological surveys and historical research that uncover where military actions took place and how soldiers, prisoners of war, civilians, and Indigenous peoples experienced these events. These efforts deepen public understanding of forgotten or lesser‑known aspects of battlefield history. 

2) Preserving Battlefield Landscapes for Future Generations - Grants support long‑term planning and preservation efforts—such as documenting battlefield terrain, updating preservation plans, and stabilizing historic structures—to ensure these important places remain protected and intact. These projects help safeguard both physical features and cultural memory for visitors today and tomorrow.

3) Creating Engaging Visitor Experiences - Funding has modernized how battlefield stories are shared. Projects have designed new exhibits, updated visitor center displays, and developed outdoor interpretive features that make complex history easier for people to explore and understand. Interactive presentations help visitors visualize key events and follow the experiences of those who lived through them.

overview.objective:
To assist States and local communities acquire and preserve threatened battlefield land from the Revolutionary War, War of 1812, and Civil War. 

This grant program enables the permanent protection of historic battlefield lands through fee simple acquisition or through the purchase of an interest in the land through a preservation covenant.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Battlefield Land Acquisition Grants support efforts to permanently protect historic battlefield lands from the Revolutionary War, War of 1812, and Civil War. This program provides competitive grants to state and local governments—often working with preservation groups—to acquire battlefield land either by purchasing it outright or through conservation easements. All grants require a dollar-for-dollar non-Federal match, ensuring communities invest alongside the federal contribution.

list.description: 1) Land Acquisition for Preservation: funding is used to acquire battlefield land that holds historical significance. This ensures the land is preserved and protected from development, maintaining its historical integrity. 2) Easement Acquisition: funds are used to acquire easements on larger tracts of land at a historic battlefield. Easements allow for the preservation of the land while still permitting certain uses, ensuring the historical landscape remains intact.

1) Permanent Protection Through Fee Simple Acquisition - funding allows communities and partner organizations to buy historic battlefield land outright so it can be permanently protected. These projects secure both large and small tracts of land that contain important terrain features, preserve the physical settings where battles occurred, and expand publicly accessible historic areas. Some acquisitions complete missing portions of a battlefield landscape, while others allow the land to be incorporated into existing parks or heritage sites. By purchasing these properties, the program ensures that battlefield lands remain safeguarded from development and available for public learning and reflection.

2) Permanent Protection Through Preservation Covenants - Funding can also be used to protect battlefield land through preservation covenants, which are legal agreements that restrict development while allowing land to remain in private ownership. These projects secure long‑term protection by working with land trusts and local partners to hold conservation easements that safeguard historic terrain, sightlines, and other features essential to understanding past conflicts. Covenants help maintain the character of battlefield landscapes, limit incompatible uses, and ensure the land remains available for future interpretation, research, and stewardship—even as ownership changes over time.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: 1) Preservation of Historical Lands: Successfully acquired and preserved numerous historically significant lands, including parcels and easements at various battlefield sites, ensuring their protection from development and maintaining their historical integrity. 2) Support for Archaeological and Historical Research: Funded archaeological surveys and historical research on newly acquired lands, leading to the discovery and documentation of important historical artifacts and features.

This program has permanently protected significant battlefield landscapes by supporting the purchase of historic land or securing long‑term preservation covenants. Through these awards, thousands of acres of important terrain have been safeguarded from development, including ridgelines, fields, approaches, and other features essential to understanding the course of past conflicts. Several projects completed the acquisition of large tracts of historically important land, while others protected smaller parcels critical to interpreting troop movements or key defensive positions. These efforts ensure that important battlefield landscapes remain intact and available for public education, stewardship, and outdoor recreation. The program has also strengthened preservation partnerships among state and local agencies, nonprofits, and land trusts. Many projects involved coordinated work to acquire battlefield properties and to hold conservation easements ensuring their long‑term protection.

To be eligible for acquisition, the land must be at least 50% within the boundary of a Revolutionary War, War of 1812 or Civil War battlefield identified in the reports above.
 
Funds may not be used to acquire land or interests in land within the legislative boundary of a unit of the National Park System. Land acquired with these funds must be preserved in perpetuity. In any case where a local government or a private non-profit organization acquires land or an interest in land with assistance from this program, it must convey an acceptable perpetual protective easement on the land to the State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) or other organization acceptable to the National Park Service and SHPO.

overview.objective: To provide matching grants for preservation or conservation work on nationally significant intellectual and cultural artifacts and nationally significant historic structures and sites. Intellectual and cultural artifacts include artifacts, collections, documents, sculpture and works of art.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Save America's Treasures funds competitive grants that help preserve and share nationally significant historic properties and cultural collections. This program supports two types of projects: 1) Preservation Projects that restore and stabilize buildings, sites, and landmarks listed on the National Register of Historic Places or recognized as National Historic Landmarks; and 2) Collections Projects that conserve important artifacts, documents, artworks, and archival materials held in museums, libraries, archives, and other cultural institutions. These grants serve a broad range of public-interest organizations—including state and local governments, nonprofit cultural organizations, college and university museums, federal agencies, and Tribal entities.

list.description: 1) Historic Preservation: Funding is often directed toward the restoration and conservation of historic buildings and landmarks, including roof, window, and masonry repairs, structural stabilization, restoration of historic interiors and facades, and preservation of historic collections and artifacts. 2) Cultural Heritage and Museums: Grants support museums and cultural institutions in conserving and digitizing collections, enhancing public access to historical exhibits, and rehabilitating historic museum buildings. 3) Community and Civic Infrastructure: Funds are used to revitalize community spaces with historical significance, such as opera houses, libraries, and town halls, enhancing accessibility and safety, and supporting adaptive reuse for public benefit. 4) Archaeological and Architectural Research: Funding may also support historic structure reports, reservation planning, and architectural services aligned with federal preservation standards.

1) Preserving historic buildings and landmarks: Repairing roofs, windows, foundations, chimneys, and exterior masonry to stop leaks, prevent structural damage, and stabilize historic buildings for long‑term public use. Strengthening interior features—such as staircases, plaster, woodwork, and finishes—so historic spaces can safely host classes, exhibits, and community gatherings. Restoring historic civic landscapes and promenades so people can experience significant public spaces as they were intended, with safe paths and renewed plantings.

2) Conserving collections and expanding public access: Conserving and digitizing rare archives and media—such as historic maps, conductor scores, quilts, oral histories, audio/video recordings, and documentary photographs—so anyone can explore them online. Rehousing artifacts in archival storage (flat files, shelving, climate control, and security upgrades) to protect items like pottery, textiles, instruments, and scientific cores from damage. Collaborating with descendant and Tribal communities to incorporate cultural perspectives into documentation and stewardship of heritage collections. Restoring historic vehicles and technology—from passenger rail cars to vintage aircraft and musical instruments—so they can be safely exhibited, interpreted, and heard or seen again by the public.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: 1) Restoring Historic Landmarks: Historic homes, churches, and civic buildings have been preserved through roof repairs, masonry restoration, and structural stabilization. 2) Revitalizing Museums and Cultural Institutions: Maritime museums, art institutions, and cultural centers have used funds to conserve, protect and display national treasures. 3)  Reopening Community Spaces: Funding has helped revive opera houses, libraries, and town halls, turning them into vibrant community hubs once again. 4) Preserving Stories and Collections: Projects have included the preservation of early American manuscripts, architectural drawings, and indigenous artifacts. 5) Protecting the Past, Building the Future: Projects have included accessibility upgrades, fire safety improvements, and energy-efficient systems, ensuring historic sites are safe and welcoming for all.

1) Safeguarding landmark buildings for public use: Sealing and stabilizing historic structures—repairing roofs, windows, foundations, and facades—to stop leaks and prevent structural failure so museums, cultural centers, and public spaces remain safe and open. Installing modern fire detection and suppression systems and upgrading electrical systems to protect large, vulnerable buildings and meet current life‑safety codes. 

2) Conserving collections and expanding access: Conserving and digitizing rare materials—historic maps, conductor scores, quilts, film and audio, photographs—so anyone can explore them online and institutions can use them for exhibits, classes, and research. Rehousing artifacts in archival storage, improving climate control and security, and creating metadata and finding aids to make collections discoverable and accessible.

overview.objective: The National Park Service – Chesapeake Bay Office aims to connect people with the Chesapeake Bay’s natural and cultural heritage by supporting conservation, public access, education, and recreation through the Chesapeake Bay Gateways and Watertrails Network. Assistance supports the implementation of the Chesapeake Bay Initiative Act, the Chesapeake Bay Program, and the Captain John Smith Chesapeake National Historic Trail. Key goals include conserving landscapes and resources, enhancing public access to waterways, promoting heritage tourism, engaging youth, and interpreting the region’s rich history and environment.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: NPS Chesapeake technical and financial assistance strategically supports projects and programs that meet DOI’s key responsibilities in the Chesapeake Bay watershed. The Chesapeake Bay Initiative Act authorizes the NPS to: identify, conserve, restore, and interpret natural, recreational, historical, and cultural resources within the Chesapeake Bay Watershed; identify and utilize the collective resources sites for enhancing public education of and access to the Chesapeake Bay; link sites with trails, tour roads, scenic byways, and other connections; develop and establish watertrails comprising water routes and connections to sites and other land resources within the Chesapeake Bay Watershed; and create a network of sites and watertrails.

list.description:
1) Water access and outdoor recreation infrastructure: Funding can build or improve paddle craft facilities and trailheads so people can reach cultural, historic, and natural sites by water. Support can add kayak and canoe launches within new public spaces, co‑designed with residents, giving tens of thousands of people safe river access for recreation and stewardship.

2) Heritage interpretation, exhibits, and museums: Funding can help museums install long‑term exhibits based on oral histories, archaeology, and community input—bringing to life rural heritage, farming, maritime work, and social change for visitors of all ages. Grants can back traveling exhibitions and milestone anniversary programs that deepen connections to the region’s heritage while supporting local economic development through cultural tourism. Funding can also expand visitor services at central heritage hubs, improving orientation, interpretation, and the overall experience so travelers stay longer and explore more.

3) Education, eco‑tours, and storytelling: Funding can create immersive, small‑group expeditions—by boat, kayak, and on land—that showcase the area’s natural and cultural heritage, partner with local farms and tourism businesses, and encourage care for waterways. Place‑based education projects can mark culturally significant river sites with signage linked to web maps and K–12 curricula, helping students and visitors understand deep local histories.

4) Trails and connectivity: Grants can complete planning and engineering for multi‑mile biking and walking trails—covering surveying, environmental and cultural studies, and easement recording—so communities can link towns, museums, and waterfronts with safe, scenic routes.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that advance the Chesapeake Bay Initiative Act of 1998 within the Chesapeake Bay watershed, including conserving landscapes and resources, enhancing public access to waterways, promoting heritage tourism, engaging youth, and interpreting the region’s rich history and environment.
