list.description:
1) Connecting People to Nature and Heritage: This program has enabled thousands of residents and visitors to experience the Chesapeake Bay’s natural beauty and cultural history. Through funding, communities have hosted festivals, music series, and educational events that celebrate local traditions, arts, and outdoor recreation. These activities draw new audiences, boost small businesses, and foster pride in local heritage.

2) Expanding Outdoor Recreation and Water Access: Grants have supported the construction and improvement of paddle craft facilities, water trailheads, and biking/walking routes. These investments make it easier for people to explore rivers, streams, and the Bay by kayak, canoe, or on foot. New launches and trail connections have opened up unique ways to visit historic sites and natural landmarks, encouraging healthy recreation and stewardship of local waterways.

3) Preserving and Interpreting History: Funding has helped museums and heritage centers install long-term exhibits based on oral histories, archaeology, and community input. These exhibits bring to life rural heritage, farming, maritime industries, and social change, offering visitors a deeper understanding of the region’s past. Traveling exhibitions and milestone anniversary programs have also strengthened cultural tourism and local economies.

4) Inspiring Environmental Stewardship: The program has launched immersive educational expeditions—by boat, kayak, and on land—that showcase the Bay’s natural and cultural heritage. These experiences connect people to local farms, historic sites, and conservation efforts, encouraging care for waterways and sustainable tourism. Community events like “Water Week” distribute native plants and engage the public in watershed protection, supporting cleaner water and expanded access to open spaces.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that advance the Chesapeake Bay Initiative Act of 1998 within the Chesapeake Bay watershed, including conserving landscapes and resources, enhancing public access to waterways, promoting heritage tourism, engaging youth, and interpreting the region’s rich history and environment.

It is the responsibility of the award recipient to comply with the Architectural Barriers Act of 1968, Section 504 and 508 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, as amended, and the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 as amended.

All projects proposed to develop new or enhanced public water access facilities must develop one or more of the following types of public water access facilities: boat-related access, swimming access, fishing access and/or viewing access for water, wildlife, and shoreline areas.

For proposed development projects located on the Captain John Smith Chesapeake National Historic Trail, NPS Chesapeake Office may supply standardized CAJO trail-marking and orientation, and possibly interpretation, signage appropriate to the site.

title: Youth and Veteran Organizations Conservation Activities

overview.objective: This program seeks to utilize qualified non-profit youth and veteran serving organizations to carry out appropriate natural and cultural resource conservation, education, and volunteer service projects on Department of the Interior lands through authorized National Park Service programs.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Youth and Veteran Organizations Conservation Activities program helps young adults and veterans gain hands‑on experience protecting and caring for America’s public lands. Through partnerships with nonprofit and community organizations, the program supports projects that strengthen conservation skills, expand volunteerism, and build pathways to careers in natural and cultural resource stewardship. This program serves youth ages 18–30, veterans up to age 35, and the community organizations that work with them.

list.description:
1. Conservation Activities: Projects support youth organizations in conservation activities such as habitat restoration, invasive species management, and trail maintenance to preserve and enhance natural landscapes.

2. Historic Preservation: Projects engage youth in the preservation of historic buildings and structures, such as restoring historic trails, maintaining old buildings, and conducting archeological research to protect cultural heritage.

3. Environmental Education: Projects supports programs that engage youth in environmental education through activities like summer camps, interpretive programs, and educational hikes. These programs aim to foster a conservation ethic and provide educational opportunities related to natural and cultural resources.

4. Wildlife Monitoring: Projects support internships and youth programs focused on wildlife monitoring. Activities include tracking wildlife populations, conducting field research, and collecting data to inform conservation strategies.

5. Infrastructure Maintenance: Projects support the maintenance and improvement of park infrastructure, such as repairing trails, maintaining campgrounds, and improving visitor facilities.

1. Trail and Facility Maintenance: Funding supports maintenance on trails, roads, and visitor attractions, as well as conservation and restoration projects. This includes deferred, cyclic, and corrective maintenance to improve public access and resource conditions.

2. Vegetation Management: Projects may involve removing invasive species, restoring native plant communities, and monitoring ecological health. Activities can include manual, mechanical, or chemical treatments, as well as seed collection and planting for habitat restoration.

3. Historic Structure Preservation: Funding is used for preservation trades training and hands-on work such as carpentry, masonry, traditional roofing, and stabilization of historic buildings and infrastructure.

4. Interpretive Programming: Funding supports the development and delivery of educational programs for visitors, including guided tours, curriculum-based activities for schools, and public outreach events. These programs aim to increase awareness of natural and cultural resources.

5. Ecological and Cultural Resource Surveys: Funding is used for monitoring water quality, wildlife populations, and plant communities, as well as conducting archaeological and historical research. Data collection supports management decisions and resource protection.

6. Community Outreach: Projects engage local communities through events, partnerships, and collaborative conservation efforts, and helps develop and coordinate volunteer opportunities.

list.description: Youth organizations have successfully restored natural habitats and managed invasive species; helped restore historic trails and buildings, ensuring these cultural landmarks are preserved for future generations; engaged in environmental education programs, fostering a conservation ethic; tracked wildlife populations and collected data, contributing to conservation strategies and wildlife management plans; participated in community outreach and assistance programs; and repaired trails, maintained campgrounds, and improved visitor facilities, ensuring safe and accessible park amenities.

Youth participants have completed a wide range of impactful projects, from rehabilitating historic irrigation systems that preserve cultural heritage to restoring trails and park infrastructure that improve safety and access for millions of visitors. They have removed invasive species, planted native vegetation, and supported wildfire recovery by stabilizing soils and reseeding damaged landscapes. Interns have also created bilingual educational materials, produced digital content, and led engaging public programs on topics like wildlife conservation and civil rights history, helping communities connect with the stories and science behind public lands. Through this work, young people have gained valuable skills, strengthened local communities, and improved the health and resilience of natural and cultural resources nationwide.

title: Preservation of Historic Structures on the Campuses of Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).

overview.objective: In 1988, the National Park Service established the Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU) Preservation grant program to document, preserve, and stabilize structures on HBCU campuses. The HBCU grant program exists to repair historic structures on campuses of Historically Black Colleges and Universities that are listed in or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places either individually or as contributing to a National Register historic district. Projects must meet major program selection criteria and all work must meet the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program provides competitive grants to accredited Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) to help preserve and protect historic buildings and structures on their campuses. Many HBCU campuses contain nationally significant historic resources that reflect the history of Black education in the United States. The program supports projects that document, stabilize, repair, and rehabilitate these historic places so they can continue to serve their institutions and communities. The program serves accredited HBCUs that own or steward historic properties listed in, or eligible for listing in, the National Register of Historic Places.

list.description: 1) Preserving Historic Campus Buildings: Funding is used to repair and restore historic buildings on the campuses of Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). These efforts include: roof replacements to prevent water damage, window and door restoration to maintain architectural integrity, and masonry and structural repairs to stabilize aging buildings. 2) Upgrading Infrastructure for Safety and Accessibility: Grants support modernizing historic structures while preserving their character. Projects include: installing elevators and ramps to improve accessibility, upgrading HVAC, plumbing, and electrical systems for safety and efficiency, and fire safety improvements such as alarms and suppression systems. 3) Stabilizing and Documenting Historic Sites: funds are used to prevent further deterioration and document historic significance, including laser scanning and drone imagery to create digital models of buildings, developing preservation plans for long-term care, and emergency stabilization of buildings at risk of collapse.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that document, preserve, stabilize, and rehabilitate historic structures located on accredited HBCU campuses. Eligible projects focus on historic resources that are listed or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, either individually or as part of a historic district.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: 1) Restoring Historic Buildings: A historic chapel, once the heart of campus gatherings, is being restored with new roofing and structural reinforcements to ensure it remains a beacon for future generations. 2) Making Campuses More Accessible: A former dormitory is being transformed into a fully accessible student center, blending historic charm with inclusive design. 3) Protecting Cultural Heritage: A university is using cutting-edge technology to digitally preserve four historic buildings, ensuring their stories are never lost—even if the structures face future threats. 4) Reviving Spaces for Learning and Community: A 1920s-era library is being transformed into a state-of-the-art archive and museum dedicated to African American history and culture.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that document, preserve, stabilize, and rehabilitate historic structures located on accredited HBCU campuses. Eligible projects focus on historic resources that are listed or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, either individually or as part of a historic district.

selectionCriteria.description:
Specific evaluation criteria will be included in the funding announcements posted on www.grants.gov.

NPS will evaluate and consider only those applications that separately address each of the merit review criteria. Each applicant is required to provide a detailed project description of the following criteria elements.

Criterion 1 - Significance

Describe the historic resource(s) in the proposed project and the role played in the Historic Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU) experience. Discuss National Register significance and the integrity of the resource. Describe how the project will result in the recognition, understanding, and preservation of the resource and the HBCU story. 

Criterion 2 – Severity of Threat to Property

Describe the current condition of the historic property and explain how it is threatened or endangered. The source(s), nature, extent, and severity of the threat, danger or damage to the property must be clearly and convincingly argued. 

Criterion 3 – Mitigation of Threat to Property

Projects must substantially mitigate or eliminate the threat, danger, or damage described and must have a clear public benefit (for example, historic places open for visitation or public use). Clearly state what preservation activities will be undertaken as part of this project.

Criterion 4 - Feasibility

The project must be feasible (i.e. able to be completed within the proposed activities, schedule, and budget described in the application). The application must: 

1. Describe how the project will result in the recognition, understanding, and preservation of associated resources. Describe any public-private partnerships involved in the project and how these partnerships will sustain and continue to support the resource(s) after the grant project is complete. Describe how the public will be actively involved in the project. 

Provide a timeline for project completion. Should your application be successful, the period of support will be negotiated by you and the funding agency but is typically 2-3 years. No work undertaken before a grant is awarded will be supported by grant funds.

title: Preservation of Japanese American Confinement Sites

overview.objective: The program provides for the preservation and interpretation of historic confinement sites where Japanese Americans were detained during World War II. The program was established to encourage projects that identify, research, evaluate, interpret, protect, restore, repair, and acquire historic confinement sites in order that present and future generations may learn and gain inspiration from these sites and that these sites will demonstrate the Nation's commitment to equal justice under the law.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports efforts to preserve and share the history of the mass removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II. It provides funding to organizations that protect historic sites, record personal stories, and create educational tools that help the public understand what happened and why it matters today. The program serves communities, educators, museums, historians, descendants, and anyone seeking to learn about civil liberties, resilience, and the lived experiences of those affected.

list.description:
1) Restoring and Interpreting Historic Spaces: Designing and installing permanent exhibits inside restored historic structures, such as an underground food‑storage cellar built by incarcerated people. These exhibits use photos, films, written records, and personal stories to help visitors understand daily life and labor. Transforming outdoor areas into reflective public spaces, including engraving thousands of names onto reclaimed building tiles and creating landscaped courtyards that honor both the people once held there and the deeper Indigenous history of the region.

2) Conducting Archaeology and Field Research: Completing multi‑season archaeological excavations to identify artifacts, document structures, and uncover material evidence of confinement. Findings are then shared through museum exhibits, public talks, and traveling displays. Combining archival records with field studies to develop accurate, publicly accessible interpretations of little‑known detention sites.

3) Digitizing and Preserving Community History: Creating nationwide “scanning days” where families can bring photos, letters, and documents to be digitized, indexed, and added to public archives. Digitizing tens of thousands of historical items — including documents, photos, and personal collections — and publishing them in online repositories.

4) Creating Educational Tools, Lessons, and Teacher Training: Building large, user‑friendly digital platforms that combine maps, encyclopedias, archival records, and new technologies to support teachers with ready‑to‑use materials. Developing leadership workshops, professional development programs, place‑based learning opportunities, and a network for teachers to collaborate across regions.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that identify, research, evaluate, interpret, protect, restore, repair and acquire historic Japanese American confinement sites. Eligible projects may also include documentation (such as archaeological surveys or National Register nominations), oral history collection, educational and interpretive media, preservation and rehabilitation of historic structures, planning efforts, and limited real property acquisition at authorized sites.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Preserving Historic Places and Cultural Landscapes: This program has helped safeguard important historic spaces connected to Japanese American wartime incarceration. Funding has supported the restoration of unique structures—such as an underground food‑storage cellar—paired with new exhibits that use photos, film, written records, and firsthand accounts to help visitors understand daily life under confinement. Projects have also revitalized historic outdoor spaces, installing engraved memorial elements, lighting, and landscaping that honor both incarcerated families and the Indigenous heritage of surrounding lands.

2) Uncovering History Through Archaeology and Research: Awarded projects have filled crucial gaps in public knowledge by conducting multi‑season archaeological digs, archival investigations, and cultural landscape studies. These efforts have uncovered building remains, artifacts, and newly documented histories from lesser‑known confinement sites. Advanced tools—including LiDAR, digital elevation modeling, and remote sensing—have been used to map areas that were once hidden, restricted, or undocumented, resulting in the first comprehensive surveys of historically significant locations. Findings are shared through museum exhibits, public talks, online content, videos, and detailed research reports.

3) Digitizing and Preserving Community Memory: The program has enabled the digitization and public release of tens of thousands of historical photos, letters, and documents. Community “scanning days” have helped families preserve fragile personal collections while contributing to national repositories. Organizations have expanded online encyclopedias, archives, and digital platforms by adding newly digitized materials, new research findings, and fresh oral histories—ensuring these resources remain publicly accessible for educators, researchers, descendants, and the broader public.

4) Strengthening National Education and Teacher Training: Funding has supported robust educational initiatives that reach teachers and students nationwide. Projects have created user‑friendly digital portals that combine archival materials, maps, and multimedia content into single accessible platforms. Traveling workshops and professional development programs provide educators with accurate historical context and ready‑to‑use classroom materials. Leadership trainings, teacher networks, and field‑based learning experiences have helped hundreds of teachers integrate place‑based and inquiry‑driven approaches to understanding this history.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that identify, research, evaluate, interpret, protect, restore, repair and acquire historic Japanese American confinement sites. Eligible projects may also include documentation (such as archaeological surveys or National Register nominations), oral history collection, educational and interpretive media, preservation and rehabilitation of historic structures, planning efforts, and limited real property acquisition at authorized sites.

assistanceUsage.description:
Japanese American Confinement Sites grant funds may be used for identifying, researching, evaluating, interpreting, protecting, restoring, repairing, and acquiring historic confinement sites where Japanese Americans were detained during World War II as authorized by the Preservation of Japanese American Confinement Sites Act of 2006. 

These historic confinement sites are defined as the ten War Relocation Authority camps (Gila River, Granada (Amache), Heart Mountain, Jerome, Manzanar, Minidoka, Poston, Rohwer, Topaz, and Tule Lake), as well as other historically significant locations, as determined by the Secretary of the Interior, where Japanese Americans were detained during World War II.

These sites are specifically identified in Confinement and Ethnicity: An Overview of World War II Japanese American Relocation Sites, published by the Department of the Interior, National Park Service, Western Archeological and Conservation Center, in 1999. For further information, Please contact the Regional Office.

The Secretary may provide financial assistance to encourage participation in the acquisition, protection, operation, development, or maintenance of such trails.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
Program supports preservation, protection, and development of the National Trails System. It provides financial assistance for projects that help operate, maintain, and enhance National Scenic, National Historic, and National Recreation Trails. Funding supports activities that keep these nationally significant trail corridors safe, accessible, and culturally and environmentally respectful.  The program helps partners carry out work such as trail operation and maintenance, resource protection, planning and trail development, interpretation and educational activities, and efforts that improve public understanding and enjoyment of the trails.

Trail‑related digital platforms, data collection systems, and public outreach tools may also be supported to improve trail information, stewardship outcomes, and long‑term sustainability. Beneficiaries include the general public, nonprofit organizations, Tribal and community partners, landowners, and state and local governments. The program emphasizes volunteer engagement and supports partners working both inside and outside federally administered areas

list.description:
1) Trail Maintenance and Infrastructure: Funding is used to repair and improve trail infrastructure, including: rehabilitating eroded trail sections, replacing or repairing footbridges, shelters, and privies, and installing erosion control structures and signage.

2) Conservation and Resource Protection: Funding is used to focus on preserving natural and cultural resources along trail corridors, including: removing invasive species and restoring native habitats, protecting historic landmarks and landscapes, and conducting environmental assessments and planning.

3) Volunteer and Youth Engagement: Funding supports volunteer programs and youth involvement, including: training and coordinating thousands of trail volunteers, and providing leadership and safety training for trail stewards.

4) Education and Interpretation: Funding helps create educational programs and interpretive materials, including developing classroom resources and field trips for students, hosting public events and reenactments, and creating signage, exhibits, and digital content to share trail history.

Building capacity for non-federal partners to protect, develop, and promote historic trails; fellows contribute to community outreach, trail planning, interpretation, and special projects that improve public awareness and support. 

Standardized data collection & reporting. Create a pilot system to collect and report, annually, trail development metrics, partnership activities, land protection progress, visitor experience conditions, and stewardship outcomes across participating managers, using the results to promote the trail, track milestones, enhance the corridor, and guide future investments. 

Digital platform maintenance & improvement. Maintain and enhance online platforms that provide history, maps, educational materials, and trip-planning information for trail users, ensuring content accuracy, cultural respect, security, open access, and long-term sustainability through regular updates, reporting, and planning

list.description:
1) Maintaining and Improving Trails - Several miles of heavily eroded trail were stabilized with new erosion-control structures, and aging footbridges and shelters were replaced to improve safety for hikers.

2) Protecting Natural and Cultural Resources - Volunteers cleared invasive species and restored native plants along a historic trail segment, while interpretive signage was installed to educate visitors about the area's cultural significance.

3) Educating and Engaging the Public - Students participated in immersive field trips along historic trails, learning about the American Revolution and Indigenous history through reenactments and storytelling.

4) Innovating with Technology - A project captured 360-degree imagery of a scenic trail, allowing people to explore it virtually and helping planners identify areas needing maintenance.

Expanding Public Access and Enjoyment. The program has enabled the operation, development, and maintenance of nationally significant trails, making them safer, more accessible, and enjoyable for millions of visitors. Projects have improved trail conditions, signage, and facilities, directly enhancing the public’s experience. 

Strengthening Partnerships and Volunteer Engagement. Supported collaborative initiatives that empower non-federal partners, volunteers, and community organizations. These efforts have increased capacity for trail stewardship, community outreach, and special projects, fostering a sense of shared responsibility and pride. 

Protecting Natural and Cultural Resources. Funding has been used to preserve and protect trail corridors, landscapes, and historic sites. Projects include land protection, resource stewardship, and collaboration with Tribal nations and local communities to ensure trails remain accessible and environmentally sound. 

Innovating with Digital Platforms and Data Systems. The program has supported the creation and maintenance of digital platforms that provide history, maps, educational materials, and tourism information. These resources are kept accurate, secure, and freely accessible, helping the public learn about and plan visits to trails. 

Enhancing Public Awareness and Education. Through interpretive programming, educational outreach, and community events, the program has increased public understanding of the significance of national trails. Fellows and partners have worked with nonprofit associations to deliver interpretation, planning, and special projects that build support for trail conservation. 

Measuring and Reporting Impact.  Awards have enabled standardized, annual data collection and reporting systems that track trail development, partnership activities, land protection progress, visitor experience conditions, and stewardship outcomes. This data guides future investments and helps promote the trail network

overview.objective: The purpose of the Heritage Partnership Program funding is to carry out programs and projects that engage National Heritage Area (NHA) recipients, partners, communities, and/or visitors in shared environmental stewardship. It promotes greater public and private participation in preservation, conservation, education, and outdoor recreation programs and activities, and builds resource stewardship ethics in is participants. Goals for each National Heritage Area are set forth in each of their designation legislation, but in general, the goal of designation as a National Heritage Area is to preserve and interpret for the educational and inspirational benefit of present and future generations the unique and significant contributions to our national heritage. This heritage is shown through certain historic and cultural lands, waterways, and structures. By preserving and interpreting this heritage, NHAs are able to encourage a broad range of economic opportunities enhancing the quality of life within the designated area, and provide a management framework to assist state/local government entities, non-profits, and others in developing policies and programs that will preserve, enhance, and interpret the cultural, historical, natural, recreation, and scenic resources of the heritage area.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Heritage Partnership Program provides federal support to National Heritage Areas to preserve, interpret, and enhance nationally significant natural, cultural, historic, and recreational resources. It funds projects that strengthen environmental stewardship, promote public and private participation in preservation and education, and improve quality of life within designated heritage regions.

Goals for each National Heritage Area are set forth in each of their designation legislation, but in general, the goal of designation as a National Heritage Area is to preserve and interpret for the educational and inspirational benefit of present and future generations the unique and significant contributions to our national heritage.

list.description:
1. Community Engagement and Heritage Preservation - Funding supports projects that bring together local communities, partners, and visitors to care for historic and cultural resources. These projects include educational programs, outreach initiatives, and events that celebrate local traditions and history. Activities may involve creating signage, hosting lectures, and developing materials that help people navigate and appreciate their surroundings.

2. Environmental Stewardship and Outdoor Recreation - Funding is used to promote environmental stewardship by encouraging public and private participation in conservation and outdoor recreation. Projects may include restoring native landscapes, maintaining trails, and organizing outdoor activities that connect people to nature and teach them about local ecosystems.

3. Economic Development and Tourism - Funding helps boost local economies by supporting heritage tourism and community events. Projects may involve marketing outreach, developing tourism infrastructure, and providing financial support to local organizations and staff. These efforts attract visitors, create jobs, and strengthen regional identity.

4. Conservation and Resource Management - Funding supports the conservation of natural, scenic, and cultural resources. Projects may include preserving historic sites, protecting watersheds, and managing parks or trails. These efforts ensure that important resources are maintained for future generations and that communities have access to recreational and educational opportunities.

1. Community Heritage and Education - Funding supports programs that engage local communities, partners, and the public in caring for historic resources. These programs provide opportunities for economic growth, inspire civic engagement, and build community pride. Activities include planning commemorative events, educational programs, and outreach to encourage participation in preservation, conservation, and outdoor recreation.

2) Public Education on History - Funding is used to support operations that educate the public about important historical figures and events. This includes staff, partners, interpretive programs, and media. Projects are designed to teach people about history through annual work plans, ensuring all activities align with the goals set by Congress.

3) Conservation and Interpretation - Funding helps preserve and interpret significant natural, historic, scenic, and cultural resources. Programs are managed by nonprofit groups, universities, state agencies, or municipal authorities. Activities include educational initiatives, strengthening collaboration among partners, and promoting a shared sense of regional identity. These efforts also support heritage tourism and maintain local and private land ownership.

4) Resource Stewardship and Ethics - Funding promotes conservation of local resources through partnerships. Programs encourage stewardship ethics in participants, including the public, nonprofits, private entities, and communities. Activities may involve conservation, education, and recreation, all managed by organizations that are not part of the federal government.

list.description:
Preserving Revolutionary War History in New Jersey -
The program works closely with local partners to protect and share New Jersey’s many Revolutionary War sites. This includes contributing to Revolution NJ, the state’s official commemoration of the nation’s 250th anniversary. These efforts help communities tell their stories, welcome visitors, and stimulate local economies through increased tourism.

Supporting the Abraham Lincoln National Heritage Area -
Funding helps sustain the operational backbone of the Abraham Lincoln NHA, its staff, partner network, preservation projects, and educational media. Each year, the recipient develops and carries out a work plan dedicated to teaching the public about Abraham Lincoln’s life and legacy. This includes interpretive programs, historic preservation activities, and community engagement initiatives.

Advancing Education and Stewardship in the Journey Through Hallowed Ground Stretching from Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to Charlottesville, Virginia, this National Heritage Area highlights landscapes and stories central to American history.

Across all National Heritage Areas, the program promotes collaboration among nonprofits, universities, municipalities, state agencies, and community groups. These partnerships help protect natural, scenic, cultural, and historic resources without federal land ownership or regulation.

Through events, educational activities, outdoor recreation opportunities, and preservation projects, the program encourages residents and visitors to connect with the places that shaped the nation. This fosters stewardship, civic engagement, and a shared sense of identity rooted in local stories and landscapes.

title: Mississippi National River and Recreation Area State and Local Assistance

overview.objective: The Mississippi National River and Recreation Area is rich with historical and cultural stories. This program provides grants for the acquisition and development within the Recreation Area of lands and waters or interests therein and provides cooperative agreements and/or technical assistance to enhance partner organization planning for and interpretation of non-Federal publicly owned lands within the Recreation Area.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This Assistance Listing is dedicated specifically to the 72‑mile Mississippi River corridor that flows through the Twin Cities region. It focuses on collaborative, community‑based conservation and encourages shared management through cooperative agreements and grants. Projects supported under this program help balance recreation, ecological health, cultural heritage, and urban community needs in one of the most significant urban national park units in the country.

list.description: Funding supports the removal of abandoned and hazardous structures from newly acquired park and trail lands, returning these areas to natural open space. This includes activities like hazardous material abatement, demolition, utility removal, and land grading. Projects include seeding native plants and trees, improving wildlife habitat, and potentially restoring prairie and shoreline ecosystems. These efforts promote biodiversity and ecological resilience.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that focus on community‑based conservation. Past funding supported improvements to outdoor recreation areas, public safety, and natural resource restoration. These projects focused on making community trails safer, restoring newly acquired open space, improving wildlife habitat, and supporting long‑term maintenance of public lands.

list.description: A recently acquired park and trail area is being transformed into a safe, welcoming, and ecologically rich public space. Old, unsafe structures are being removed to eliminate hazards and restore the land to its natural state. This includes clearing debris, sealing wells, removing outdated utilities, and reshaping the land for future use. Once cleared, the land is being revitalized with native trees, grasses, and prairie plants. New trails and access points are being developed to invite the public to explore and enjoy the outdoors.
Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that support the Recreation Area of lands and waters or interests therein.

overview.objective:
The Natural Resource Stewardship program is the principle means through which the National Park Service (NPS) evaluates and improves the health of watersheds, landscapes, and marine and coastal resources, sustains biological communities on the lands and waters in parks, and actively endeavors to improve the resiliency of these natural resources.
 
NPS conducts natural resource stewardship largely at the park level, utilizing park personnel and contractor or cooperative support. To carry out and further this stewardship responsibility, the NPS implements programs that encompass a broad range of research, operational, and educational activities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program provides federal financial assistance to eligible recipients to support conservation, research, restoration, and resource‑management activities that enhance natural resources managed by the National Park Service. Eligible applicants include tribal governments, state and local agencies, nonprofit organizations, institutions of higher education, and other qualified entities. Supported activities may include ecological research, habitat restoration, invasive‑species management, wildlife monitoring, public education, and stewardship actions aligned with federal priorities. The program emphasizes collaborative partnerships and science‑based approaches that deliver measurable public benefits.

list.description:
1) Restoring Native Habitats and Wildlife - Funding supports the restoration of endangered plant species and the reintroduction of native vegetation in areas affected by wildfires or invasive species. This includes growing native plants, removing harmful species, and monitoring wildlife recovery.

2) Protecting Aquatic Ecosystems - Funds are used to monitor fish populations, restore riverbanks, and improve water quality in national parks. These efforts help maintain healthy aquatic habitats and support species that rely on clean water.

3) Monitoring Birds and Wildlife - Projects involve tracking bird populations using acoustic recorders or field surveys. The data helps scientists understand changes in wildlife behavior and habitat use.

4) Supporting Scientific Research and Data Collection - Projects fund long-term ecological monitoring, including vegetation surveys, impact studies, and data analysis. The results guide park management decisions and contribute to national databases.

1) Restoring Habitats and Wildlife - Funding helps repair damaged natural areas by removing invasive plants, planting native vegetation, and supporting the recovery of wildlife after disturbances like wildfires. These efforts improve ecosystem health and create safer, more resilient landscapes.

2) Protecting Water and Aquatic Life - Funds support monitoring and restoring rivers, streams, and wetlands. Activities may include improving water quality, studying fish populations, and stabilizing riverbanks to keep aquatic habitats healthy for plants, animals, and visitors.

3) Monitoring Birds and Other Wildlife - Projects may track birds and other species using tools such as field surveys or audio recorders. The information collected helps scientists understand wildlife movements, nesting behavior, health trends, and how species use their habitat.

4) Supporting Science and Long‑Term Research - Funding supports ongoing ecological studies—like vegetation surveys, monitoring, and data collection—to guide park management decisions. This research helps maintain healthy natural areas and contributes to national conservation data.

list.description:
1) Restoring Native Landscapes - Teams are removing invasive plants and reintroducing native vegetation to restore balance in fragile ecosystems. This includes planting native grasses and wildflowers that support pollinators and wildlife.

2) Protecting Birds and Their Habitats - Specialists are monitoring endangered and migratory bird species to understand their nesting patterns, migration routes, and population health. This includes using acoustic recorders and field surveys to track changes over time.

3) Safeguarding Aquatic Ecosystems - Scientists are studying rivers, streams, and coastal areas to monitor water quality and aquatic life. Restoration projects are improving fish habitats and protecting water sources.

4) Advancing Scientific Research - Research teams are studying everything from ancient ice age landscapes to the genetics of rare species. These projects often involve universities and nonprofit organizations working alongside park scientists.

1) Restoring Healthy Ecosystems - Funding supports hands‑on projects that restore forests, wetlands, rivers, and coastal habitats. For example, partners work with scientists to collect native plant seeds, grow them in nurseries, and replant them in damaged areas to help ecosystems recover and thrive. These projects improve soil stability, restore native plant communities, and rebuild habitats for wildlife.

2) Protecting Native Species - Funding helps ensure that restoration projects use plants uniquely adapted to local conditions. By selecting genetically appropriate seeds and cultivating them over several growing seasons, teams develop strong native stock that can withstand floods, storms, pests, and changing conditions. This approach strengthens ecosystem resilience and supports long‑term biodiversity.

3) Rehabilitating Rivers and Waterways - Funding assists efforts to protect and enhance river corridors, estuaries, and streamside areas. Projects involve improving water quality, stabilizing riverbanks with native vegetation, and reconnecting communities with their waterways through educational stewardship events. These activities help fish and wildlife, make water systems more resilient, and support cleaner, healthier environments.

4) Supporting Community Stewardship - Projects funded often engage volunteers, students, and residents in hands‑on conservation activities. Examples include planting native trees, removing invasive species, restoring pollinator habitat, and maintaining outdoor spaces. These efforts deepen public understanding of natural resource protection and build lasting connections between people and the land.

title: Cooperative Research and Training Programs – Resources of the National Park System

overview.objective:
To establish and maintain cooperative study units, in partnership with federal, state, and local governments, tribes, nonprofit organizations, and institutions of higher education, to facilitate multi-disciplinary science and integrated information products related to the resources of the National Park System. 
 
To maintain a comprehensive network of cooperative study units that provide full geographic and topical coverage for research, technical assistance, and educational activities related to the resources within units of the National Park System and their larger regions.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Cooperative Research and Training Programs support a nationwide network of university‑based study units that work with the National Park Service to address natural and cultural resource challenges. 

Through collaborative research, technical assistance, and education, the program helps develop practical, science‑based information that improves stewardship of parks and their surrounding landscapes.

This assistance listing strengthens partnerships between academic institutions, researchers, students, and resource managers by funding projects that study wildlife, plants, water, air quality, historic sites, and other park resources. It also provides training opportunities for students and emerging professionals, expanding the scientific and technical workforce needed to care for public lands.

The program serves state and local governments, tribal governments, nonprofit organizations, universities, conservation partners, researchers, communities, and the general public. 

What makes this program unique is its focus on cooperative, interdisciplinary science conducted through long‑standing partnerships that bring together local knowledge, academic expertise, and park management needs.

These collaborations help ensure that decisions about park resources are informed, transparent, and grounded in shared research.

list.description:
1) Environmental Research and Monitoring - Funding supports scientific studies that assess the health of ecosystems. For example: Measuring water quality in rivers and lakes to detect pollution or changes over time; monitoring bat populations to understand the spread of diseases like white-nose syndrome, and using drones to observe marine mammals in remote coastal areas.

2) Cultural and Historical Preservation - Funding is used to document and protect cultural heritage. This includes: conducting archaeological surveys to uncover and record historic sites; and preserving historic buildings through masonry repair and conservation techniques.

3) Wildlife and Habitat Restoration - Projects aim to restore natural habitats and protect endangered species. Examples include: reintroducing native plants to areas overrun by invasive species; studying rare animals like alpine wildlife or shorebirds to inform conservation strategies; and restoring coral reefs and monitoring their recovery.

4) Student Engagement and Education - Funding helps connect young people with nature and science through: internships that provide hands-on experience in conservation and park management; field schools where students learn archaeological or ecological methods; and outreach programs that bring environmental science into classrooms.

5) Data Collection and Decision Support - Some projects focus on gathering and analyzing data to guide future actions: mapping subsistence resources to support community planning and sustainability, and creating models to forecast wildlife population trends.

1) Natural Resource Conservation and Ecosystem Health - Projects include monitoring wildlife diseases and testing treatments, studying river systems to understand algae, insects, water chemistry, and habitat conditions, and modeling snowpack, weather, and watersheds to track long‑term ecological change. Teams survey rare plants, map invasive species, and assess habitat needs, while restoration specialists rebuild coastal ecosystems by re‑establishing seagrass meadows using resilient seed stock. Endangered‑species research evaluates genetics, diseases, and habitat requirements to guide recovery actions. Across large landscapes, vegetation and ecosystem‑health mapping uses imaging, satellite data, and field surveys to monitor change and support science‑based management.

2) Wildlife Monitoring and Stewardship - Projects track bats, birds, amphibians, and other species to understand population trends and how animals use their habitats. These efforts often link wildlife‑movement data with recreation patterns to help land managers balance visitor access with ecological needs. Results are shared through public‑facing education and outreach, building awareness and encouraging community involvement in protecting wildlife.

3) Cultural Resource Documentation and Protection - Projects survey archaeological and paleontological sites, update and map cultural‑resource records, and complete historic‑preservation assessments that support compliance‑ready reporting. Work also includes conserving museum collections, improving storage and cataloging, compiling cultural research, refining documentation tools, and strengthening consultation with tribal nations and local communities to ensure cultural resources are accurately represented and responsibly cared for.

4) Community Engagement and Workforce Development - Projects strengthen public connection to natural resources by creating accessible education materials, hosting volunteer events that bring people together to care for public lands, and building hands‑on pathways for young people and emerging professionals. Funding supports internships, field‑training opportunities, and research experiences that give students practical skills and real‑world exposure to conservation work. These efforts foster stewardship, deepen community involvement, and help prepare the next generation of resource‑management professionals.

list.description:
1) Scientific Research and Environmental Monitoring: Scientists are studying water quality, air pollution, and soil conditions to detect environmental changes and protect natural resources. Wildlife research projects include monitoring bat populations, studying rare foxes, and assessing the health of fish and bird species to guide conservation efforts.

2) Preserving Cultural Heritage - Teams are surveying and preserving historic buildings, archaeological sites, and cultural landscapes to ensure they are protected for future generations. Initiatives are capturing oral histories and documenting the experiences of communities, enriching our shared national story.

3) Restoring Natural Habitats - Crews are removing harmful plants and restoring native vegetation to support biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. Efforts include replanting native species and restoring wetlands, forests, and coastal areas to their natural state.

4) Student Engagement and Education - Students are gaining hands-on experience in conservation, archaeology, and environmental science through immersive programs.

Protecting Wildlife and Natural Resources:

Projects have advanced the protection of bats, birds, fish, and endangered species through disease monitoring, habitat surveys, and restoration efforts. For example, teams have tracked bat populations to combat white-nose syndrome, monitored rare amphibians and reptiles, and restored habitats for threatened shorebirds and turtles.
Research on river health, water quality, and aquatic habitats has informed management actions to keep waterways clean and support healthy fish and wildlife populations.

Preserving History and Culture:

The program has funded the documentation and preservation of historic sites, structures, and artifacts, including cataloging Revolutionary War artifacts, preserving historic buildings, and conducting oral history interviews to capture diverse stories.
Ethnographic and cultural studies have deepened understanding of the traditions and histories of Indigenous communities, African American heritage, and other groups connected to park lands.

Restoring and Managing Ecosystems:

Restoration projects have improved the health of forests, grasslands, wetlands, and coastal areas. Activities include removing invasive species, planting native vegetation, and restoring oyster reefs and seagrass meadows to benefit wildlife and protect shorelines.
Innovative research has addressed the impacts of wildfires, drought, and invasive pests, helping managers develop strategies for resilient landscapes.

Advancing Science and Education:

The program has supported hands-on internships, fieldwork, and training for students and early-career professionals, building the next generation of scientists and resource managers.
Projects have produced new tools, data, and reports, such as high-resolution maps, monitoring protocols, and public-facing educational materials, that inform park management and engage the public.

Improving Visitor Experience and Public Safety:

Visitor use studies and new technologies have helped parks better understand and manage visitor patterns, ensuring safe and enjoyable experiences.
Public safety has been enhanced through projects that secure hazardous sites, such as abandoned mines, and by developing outreach materials on wildlife and environmental risks.

Engaging Communities and Building Partnerships:

Many projects have involved local communities, volunteers, and tribal partners in stewardship, education, and research, fostering shared responsibility for park resources.
Collaborative efforts have produced best-practice guides, workshops, and public programs that connect people to parks and promote conservation.

overview.objective: The National Park Service (NPS) conducts cultural resource stewardship largely at the park level. Projects encompass a broad range of research, operational, and educational activities across all aspects of cultural resource stewardship, including but not limited to inventory, monitoring, research, rehabilitation, reconstruction, restoration, preservation, documentation, data recovery, and education.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Cultural Resources Management listing supports projects that protect, document, and share the many stories, traditions, and materials that reflect our nation’s history and cultural heritage. Through cooperative agreements, the program helps communities and organizations care for historic objects, archives, archaeological sites, cultural landscapes, and traditional practices. Funding may support activities such as surveying and documenting cultural resources, preserving fragile materials, improving public access to collections, supporting educational programs, and strengthening community stewardship of cultural traditions.
This listing serves a wide range of partners, including state and local governments, Tribal nations, nonprofit organizations, educational and scientific institutions, associations, and individuals working to preserve cultural resources for public benefit. These partners play a key role in expanding access to history, protecting culturally important places and objects, and making sure that the knowledge held in collections and cultural landscapes is passed on to future generations.

list.description:
1) Preserving Cultural Heritage - Funding supports the preservation of historic buildings, landmarks, and cultural landscapes across the country, such as stabilizing historic ranch buildings and telegraph stations to prevent further deterioration.

2) Documenting and Interpreting History - Projects aim to research, document, and share the stories of people, places, and events that shaped the nation. Examples include producing administrative histories of national parks to better understand their development and management, and conducting oral history interviews with tribal elders and community members to preserve traditional knowledge.

3) Engaging Indigenous and Local Communities - Many projects are designed to collaborate with tribal nations and local communities to ensure inclusive stewardship of cultural resources. Examples include partnering with tribal governments to document culturally significant sites and practices, and facilitating community planning meetings for new exhibits and educational programs.

1) Preservation and Access to Cultural Resources - Funding helps make historic photographs, records, and artifacts accessible to the public by digitizing images, creating standardized metadata, and sharing files online. Projects also preserve fragile items like photograph albums and scrapbooks by stabilizing them and moving them into archival storage, ensuring they remain available for researchers, educators, and the public. Special collections in libraries are inventoried and made accessible, providing up-to-date research materials for a wide range of users.
 
2) Protection and Care of Archaeological Materials - Projects support the stabilization and rehousing of archaeological materials to prevent deterioration and ensure long-term preservation. Artifacts are transferred into archival containers and documented for accurate tracking, protecting important cultural resources and supporting park research and stewardship. Projects also update archaeological surveys, document previously undocumented sites, and provide essential data for wildfire mitigation and resource management.

3) Historic Preservation and Maintenance - Funding supports apprenticeships and specialized skills training for students, veterans, and recent graduates to assist with facility management and historic preservation. Projects include carpentry, masonry, monument conservation, roofing, structural stabilization, and arboriculture, promoting safety and the preservation of treasured sites. Arborists improve conditions in historic orchards through pruning, mulching, vegetation management, and volunteer leadership, expanding opportunities for public engagement.

4) Community and Tribal Stewardship - Projects help organize ceremonies to celebrate repatriation of objects, supporting tribal communities in their stewardship of cultural heritage. Projects also facilitate access to archival materials for the public and enrich educational outreach through first-person narratives, guest speakers, and long-term exhibits. Partnerships provide mentorship and collaboration in survey, documentation, and preservation activities, supporting resource management and protecting sites.

title: National Fire Plan-Wildland Urban Interface Community Fire Assistance

overview.objective: To assist communities at risk from catastrophic wildland fires by providing assistance in the following areas: community programs that develop local capability including; assessment and planning, mitigation activities, and community and homeowner education and action; plan and implement hazardous fuels reduction activities, monitoring or maintenance associated with such hazardous fuels reduction activities, on federal land, or on adjacent nonfederal land for activities that mitigate the threat of catastrophic fire to communities and natural resources in high risk areas; enhance local and small business employment opportunities for rural communities; enhance the knowledge and fire protection capability of rural fire districts by providing assistance in education, and mitigation methods on a cost share basis; and implementing the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports communities that are at risk from devastating wildland fires by helping them strengthen their local fire resilience and preparedness. The program provides funding for community-led efforts such as wildfire risk assessments, local mitigation planning, and education that helps residents understand how to protect their homes and neighborhoods. It also supports projects that reduce hazardous vegetation and fuels, either in nearby federal areas or on surrounding non-federal lands, to lessen the threat of severe fires in high‑risk regions. In addition, the program boosts opportunities for rural workers and small businesses and improves the capabilities of local fire districts through training and modern approaches to wildfire prevention. Through these combined efforts, the program advances the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy while empowering communities, Tribal governments, states, local agencies, schools, and nonprofit organizations to build safer, more fire‑adapted places.

list.description: Funded projects focus on protecting communities and natural resources from catastrophic wildfires, including clearing hazardous vegetation along roads and trails to reduce fuel for wildfires; creating defensible space around historic structures and park facilities; conducting brush removal, pile burning, and firebreak maintenance.

Funding supports work that reduces wildfire danger and protects important historic places by cleaning up overgrown vegetation and maintaining healthier landscapes. Crews create safe buffer zones around buildings, clear brush and fallen limbs, and chip or remove dense vegetation along fences and fire breaks. These activities help safeguard cultural treasures, improve wildlife habitat, and lower the chance that intense wildfires will damage natural areas or structures.

title: National Park Service Conservation, Protection, Outreach, and Education

overview.objective:
This program supports projects complementary to National Park Service program efforts in natural and cultural resource conservation, protection, and environmental sustainability. 

This program funds projects that support the mission of the National Park Service but are not covered under other specific programs.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
This program supports projects that help care for and protect the natural and cultural resources found on public lands while expanding opportunities for people to learn about and enjoy these places. Funding may be used for activities such as restoring habitats, preserving historic features, improving visitor access, and offering educational programs that connect communities with nature, history, and science. The program also helps strengthen environmental sustainability by supporting projects that reduce impacts to sensitive resources and promote responsible outdoor recreation.
This assistance listing serves a broad group of partners, including nonprofit organizations, government entities, industry groups, researchers, and members of the public who benefit from healthier landscapes, improved access, and expanded learning opportunities.

list.description:
1)	Educational and Professional Development: Projects support teacher professional development and the creation of educational materials for distance learning, helping educators integrate public lands into their curriculum.
2)	Public Engagement and Interpretation: Funds are used to develop programs that enhance visitor enjoyment, promote interpretation of natural and cultural resources, and increase public understanding of conservation issues.
3)	Visitor Services and Transportation: Awards finance shuttle operations in high-visitation areas to reduce environmental impacts and improve access, such as those servicing forest or coastal sites.
4)	Restoration and Stewardship: Funding is directed to nonprofit partnerships for hands-on restoration work, habitat improvement, and trail maintenance to improve ecological health and visitor safety.
5)	Cultural Enrichment and Recreation: Funding may cover live music or interpretive performances to enrich visitor experiences and foster community engagement in recreational spaces.

1) Education, engagement, and access - Outdoor recreation experiences for students and military families. Facilitated trips introduce people to activities like fishing, camping, hiking, paddling, and biking, while reducing barriers such as transportation and gear. Public events provide youth‑friendly activities and demonstrations that spark interest in aviation and science.

2) Transportation and visitor services - Funding supports a visitor shuttle so sites don’t have to close when parking fills; the service expands access and improves the experience for everyone. Transit programs ease congestion, improve accessibility, and allow visitors to bring bikes or boats—reducing traffic, improving air quality, and enhancing safety.

3) Stewardship, conservation, and safety - Trail care and public‑space cleanup. Staff coordinate with site managers to remove debris and graffiti, manage vegetation, repair trail surfaces, and support safe enjoyment of historic places. Projects sample for invasive mussels, educate boaters, and conduct inspections to keep waterways healthy during high‑use seasons. Teams help with invasive species control, habitat assessments, long‑term monitoring, and restoration—building skills while advancing stewardship goals. Partnerships operate river gages and temperature sensors that provide long‑term data used for water supply management, water‑quality tracking, and flood planning.

4) National celebrations and public events - Funding supports widely viewed programs featuring orchestral performances for Memorial Day and Independence Day, for the benefit of millions. A multi‑day public event brings historic ships for parades and activities that highlight national history and strengthen international partnerships.

list.description: Assistance Listing 15.954 supports a wide range of community-driven projects that connect people to public lands. It funds teacher training and educational materials that bring parks into classrooms, helping students learn about nature and history from anywhere. Funds also support programs that enhance the visitor experience—like guided tours and exhibits that explain the importance of conservation. In busy parks, the program helps fund shuttle services to ease traffic and protect sensitive areas. It also backs restoration work led by nonprofits, improving trails, habitats, and overall safety. Cultural events like live music and performances funded through this program enrich visits and build stronger community ties to public lands.

In 2026, this program supported a wide range of projects that strengthened conservation, expanded public access, deepened community partnerships, and improved understanding of natural and cultural resources across the country. Funding helped protect waterways by preventing the spread of invasive aquatic species and supporting monitoring efforts that keep rivers and lakes healthy for wildlife and recreation. Important restoration work continued in forested and mountainous areas, where specialists collected data, planted native vegetation, assessed post‑fire conditions, and improved habitat resilience in the face of drought and wildfires.

Many achievements centered on improving visitor access and enhancing outdoor experiences. Transportation projects expanded shuttle services and public transit options, reducing congestion, improving air quality, and helping hundreds of thousands of visitors reach popular destinations safely. Parks strengthened emergency services, maintained fee‑collection operations, and improved trails and landscapes to ensure safe, enjoyable recreation for all. Educational programs introduced thousands of students and military families to outdoor activities like hiking, camping, and science-based exploration, helping people overcome barriers and feel welcome in public lands. Teachers received training to incorporate park science into classroom lessons, and youth participated in internships focused on resource management, and ecosystem stewardship.
Cultural and historic preservation also saw significant progress. Projects safeguarded historic structures, supported community-centered museum initiatives, delivered large public America 250 celebrations of national heritage, and expanded engagement.

title: Cooperative Management of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve.

overview.objective: The objectives of this program focus on the cooperative management, administration, and protection of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve. They include overseeing land and facilities, administering conservation programs, and ensuring compliance with preservation measures. The work also involves coordinating with local governments, entering into partnerships and contracts, and securing funding to support the reserve’s long-term stewardship and public engagement.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve is a unique place where history, rural landscapes, natural beauty, and community come together. Through this financial assistance program, the National Park Service works in partnership with the State of Washington and local governments to support the cooperative management of the Reserve, as directed by Public Law 95‑625. The program exists to help ensure that the Reserve’s historic farms, scenic views, cultural resources, recreational opportunities, and natural environments are protected and maintained for the benefit of the public. Unlike many national park units, Ebey’s Landing is managed through a shared governance model. The National Park Service can transfer certain management responsibilities to state or local partners, provide technical assistance, and offer supplemental funding to support day‑to‑day operations, long‑term preservation, and visitor services. These cooperative agreements strengthen local stewardship, allow communities to directly shape how the Reserve is cared for, and ensure that its rural heritage remains a living part of Island County.

title: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund
popularLongName: HPF Disaster Relief Program; Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund Grants (ESHPF)

overview.objective: The objectives of this supplemental funding is to provide for necessary expenses related to the consequences of disasters, including costs to States, Tribes, and territories. Funds may be used for historic and cultural resource preservation work in the program areas defined by the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) and that meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. Capacity, technical assistance, and emergency repairs to historic and archeological resources impacted by disasters, consistent with legislative intent, may be funded. Funding should substantially mitigate disaster caused damage and mitigate future risk.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This Assistance Listing provides disaster recovery grants to support the preservation and repair of historic and cultural resources listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or equivalent Tribal register. Funding may be used for preservation work eligible under the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) that also meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. Eligible projects include physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administrative and capacity support within areas receiving major disaster declarations. Funding should substantially mitigate disaster-caused damage and future risk.

list.description: No new awards were funded in FY 2025.

1) Emergency stabilization and repairs - Stabilizing historic buildings: Shoring up walls, roofs, and foundations; addressing water intrusion; and performing immediate repairs so structures don’t deteriorate further after storms, floods, or fires. Repairing community landmarks: Fixing damage to historic hospitals, theaters, hotels, and other public‑serving buildings so they can safely host visitors, programs, and services again.

2) Planning and assessments - Damage assessments and preservation planning: Hiring engineers and preservation specialists to inspect historic promenades, buildings, and cultural sites after declared disasters; documenting conditions and prioritizing repairs so places can reopen safely. Pre‑preservation work: Creating scopes of work, schedules, and cost estimates; coordinating with local stakeholders to plan repairs and conservation activities that meet preservation standards.

3) District‑wide recovery - Commercial district rehabilitation: Stabilizing and repairing groups of historic storefronts and civic buildings in a downtown area so small businesses can reopen and heritage corridors remain intact. Neighborhood and site‑wide efforts: Coordinating repairs across multiple historic resources within a district or campus—including hazard abatement, structural fixes, and weatherproofing—to restore public access.

4) Capacity to manage recovery - Compliance reviews and permitting support: Funding staff time to process preservation reviews required by law, helping communities move disaster‑recovery projects forward quickly and responsibly. Survey and inventory of damaged areas: Field teams document storm‑, flood‑, and fire‑impacted historic resources; results feed public databases and guide repair and mitigation. Register activities and documentation: Preparing nominations and formal records for significant places affected by disasters, strengthening recognition and long‑term protection.

financialInformation.additionalInformation: Funding is based on Congressional actions wherein appropriations are made after natural disasters.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: Provide Notice of Funding Opportunity and outreach for the award of $48 million in Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund (ESHPF) funding to be obligated in FY2026.

1) Planning and Assessments - Funding provides critical support for communities in the immediate aftermath of disasters by funding thorough assessments and preservation planning. Specialists examine damaged historic buildings, cultural sites, and public landmarks to understand the extent of harm and identify urgent stabilization needs. These assessments lead directly to carefully developed preservation plans that include scopes of work, cost estimates, and repair strategies. By investing in planning up front, communities are better equipped to protect historic resources, prevent further deterioration, and move more quickly toward safe reopening.

2) Emergency Stabilization and Repairs - Once damage is documented, funding helps stabilize and repair historic places so they remain safe and usable. This can include reinforcing weakened roofs and foundations, repairing structural components, addressing water intrusion, or restoring features that were damaged by wind, fire, or flooding. This work saves meaningful community landmarks—from historic hospitals and theaters to long‑standing hotels and religious buildings—allowing them to continue hosting programs, providing services, and anchoring local identity. Repairs also extend to historically significant infrastructure, such as railroad equipment, ensuring that hands‑on pieces of local history remain accessible for future generations.

3) District‑Wide Recovery - In many areas, a disaster affects not just a single building but entire historic districts. Funding supports coordinated, district‑wide recovery efforts that help multiple cultural properties at once. Stabilization and repair across commercial corridors allow small businesses housed in historic storefronts to reopen more quickly. Rehabilitating civic buildings and public spaces preserves the character of historic downtowns and strengthens local tourism and revitalization efforts. These comprehensive recovery projects ensure that entire communities can regain their sense of place after devastating storms, floods, or fires.

4) Capacity Building and Preservation Services - Funding strengthens the ability of states, Tribes, territories, nonprofits, and educational institutions to manage disaster‑related preservation needs. Funding helps organizations complete legally required preservation reviews, maintain updated inventories of storm‑damaged resources, and prepare documentation like National Register nominations. Many awards support training, technical assistance, and disaster planning so that local stewards know how to respond effectively when future emergencies occur. Others improve digital systems and databases used for compliance, which speeds up recovery projects and enhances transparency. These services ensure that preservation work is done responsibly, efficiently, and with long‑term resilience in mind.

description: Credentials for these programs are outlined in the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.), 36 CFR 61, the Historic Preservation Fund Grants Manual, 2 CFR 200 in its entirety, and appropriations law as enacted by Congress. In general, sites eligible for these programs must be listed in, or eligible for listing in, the National Register of Historic places.

assistanceUsage.description: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund (ESHPF) grants must be used to preserve historic and cultural resources located in areas that have received major disaster declarations and are listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or similar Tribal register. Grants assist in physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administration activities necessary to carry out the preceding activities. All funded projects must follow the applicable Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. In accordance with 54 USC 302902, grantees must agree to assume, after completion of a rehabilitation project, the cost of the continued maintenance, repair, and administration of the property in a manner satisfactory to the Secretary of the Interior. Restrictions on the use of funding are set by Congress and the parameters of the specific supplemental appropriation as well as in the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.), 36 CFR 61, the Historic Preservation Fund Grants Manual, and 2 CFR 200. Acquisition, local government certification, and tax incentives are not eligible activities. Project work must comply with what is popularly referred to as Section 106 (54 USC 306108) and Section 110 (54 USC 306107) of the National Historic Preservation Act as well as the National Environmental Policy Act (PL 91-190).
